ANYI — LS IMMERSIVE LIFE / LSPD PROJECT
MASTER HISTORY & CONTINUATION TRANSFER

Current transfer date: 22 September 2026
Purpose: preserve the project’s historical context, design decisions, production history, debugging history, current architecture, known-good behavior, known-bad revisions, and chat-section rules for the next continuation conversation.

COPY-PASTE CONTINUATION CONTEXT

You are continuing Anyi’s long-running GTA V Enhanced modding project conversation. 
The project is called LS Immersive Life / LSPD Police Authority. It grew out of an older
AnyiLSPDProject / Anyi LSPD Police Authority line and many months of iterative production,
testing, debugging, source revisions, runtime logs, and gameplay observations.

Treat the project history as a chronology, not as a bag of interchangeable files. A statement
that something was proposed, generated, tested, or called “fixed” in an earlier conversation
does NOT mean it is part of the current stable source. Source code, the actual Visual Studio
build, deployed runtime, runtime logs, and observed gameplay are the authority. Never merge
different revisions merely because two files have similar names.

Do not invent missing memories, APIs, classes, file relationships, gameplay behavior, or
historical events. When the exact historical record is unavailable, say that the record is
not established instead of guessing. Never silently migrate the project to another architecture.
Never create a second project, parallel scripts directory, scripts\scripts directory, duplicate
runtime, replacement architecture, or giant unrelated rewrite unless Anyi explicitly requests it.

This continuation must preserve Anyi’s existing project boundaries and must distinguish:
the current implementation, older implementations, experimental/broken revisions, proposed
future behavior, and user-reported gameplay behavior.

THE BEGINNING: ANYI’S OLDER LSPD PROJECT LINE

The Police project did not begin as the fully separated LS Immersive Life architecture seen
today. The earlier AnyiLSPDProject line was developed incrementally around a personal Police
Authority fantasy: Anyi enters a police role, patrols, receives police activity, investigates
incidents, interacts with civilians and suspects, requests Police support, arrests suspects,
transports prisoners, and eventually returns to normal GTA gameplay.

The old project accumulated many individual systems and repeated revisions. That history is
important because later production repeatedly encountered the same fundamental engineering
problem: files from different generations could look compatible while actually belonging to
different contracts. A newer Dispatch or Convoy source could expect fields or methods that an
older Core/Profile/Config source did not contain. This produced compiler cascades, duplicated
behavior, broken ownership, and runtime instability.

The project therefore gradually moved toward a much stricter ownership model. The Police
Authority layer became the central gameplay owner, while individual systems became owners of
their own actors and lifecycle. This was not merely a naming change. It became one of the
most important architectural lessons of the entire production history: an actor should have
one clear task owner at a time, and a support system should not secretly take ownership of
another system’s entities.

THE TRANSITION INTO LS IMMERSIVE LIFE

The LS Immersive Life project was developed as the more organized continuation of that
Police Authority idea. The goal became a believable Police gameplay layer inside GTA V
Enhanced rather than a collection of unrelated scripts.

The main player-facing route became a Roleplay gateway leading into Police Authority.
LSIMMERSIVEUI / LSImmersiveLifeMainUI acts as the gateway. LSRoleplay handles role selection.
LSAuthorityRole routes the Police role. LSImmersivePoliceUI is the Police gameplay interface,
while LSImmersivePoliceCore is the central Police orchestration layer. LSPDAuthority controls
the Police environment and authority state, including wanted-level behavior. LSPDPoliceResponse
handles normal responding Police NPCs. LSPDBackUp handles player-requested support units.
LSPDDispatch and LSPDDispatchEvent own Dispatch. LSPDCrimeActivity and its event layer own
Crime Activity. LSPDConvoy owns the physical prisoner transport/station journey. LSPDPatrol
owns patrol/on-duty state. LSPDProfile owns the Police profile/loadout. LSImmersiveMainConfig
is the universal configuration layer. LSImmersiveLog owns runtime logging.

The project also developed a dedicated civilian interaction owner, LSPDNPCResponse, plus
LSNPCDatabase and LSNPCDatabase.xml for citizen records/generation. Criminal activity assets
were moved toward the LSPDCRIMINALPROFILE.xml database rather than being repeatedly hard-coded
inside activity code. Gang integration remained deliberately read-only through the existing
Gang & Turf data integration/adapter boundary.

THE CORE DESIGN PHILOSOPHY THAT EMERGED

A major theme of the production history was separation of ownership. Dispatch owns a
Dispatch incident. Convoy owns the prisoner and physical transport. Crime Activity owns
its criminal scene. NPC Response owns the selected civilian contact. Gang & Turf owns its
gang actors. Police Backup owns only the Police units it spawned and the bounded support
assignment. Ambient GTA Police is not supposed to be silently converted into Anyi’s private
Backup.

This ownership model was repeatedly reinforced because earlier versions suffered from tasks
fighting each other. A follow task could overwrite combat. A combat task could be overwritten
by a route task. A passenger could fail to return to Follow. Weapon profiles could be reapplied
continuously. A support unit could accidentally be sent through a generic route loop after it
had already entered a specialized scene. The later architecture therefore treats task
ownership and lifecycle boundaries as first-class rules.

POLICE AUTHORITY, UI, PATROL AND CONTROLS

The intended Police gameplay flow became deliberately direct. Entering Police Mode should
lead naturally into the Police Authority gameplay UI rather than forcing Anyi through
redundant menus. The Police Mode/Authority route should load the Police data and expose the
actual gameplay interface.

Patrol is not meant to be a decorative state. Activating Patrol should put the Police system
into an active patrol state so Dispatch, NPC observation, Gang observation, and other Police
activity can begin according to their own conditions. The UI should not require repetitive
menu clicking just to reach the operational Police layer.

The project uses contextual controls. The historical controller design centered on X as
Yes/Accept/Agree and O as No/Reject/Disagree, with keyboard controls secondary and configurable.
The keyboard scheme that became part of the project history uses Y for Yes/Agree and N for
No/Disagree. Backspace and Escape are navigation/cancel controls and must never accidentally
count as a rejection. Input should use deliberate press/rising-edge behavior rather than
repeating every frame while a button remains held.

The project also accumulated practical Police conveniences: GPS to the Police station,
GPS to the active incident, GPS to prison, station markers, Police radio, emergency signals,
and contextual UI. The UI is intended to remain readable and hierarchical rather than
becoming a giant configuration simulator.

DISPATCH AND SUSPECT LIFECYCLE HISTORY

Dispatch evolved into a real stateful lifecycle: a call can be offered, accepted, travelled
to, investigated, escalated into a pursuit or scene response, resolved, and then completed
cleanly so the next activity can become available.

One recurring historical problem was the 'statue suspect'. A Dispatch-owned suspect could
exist in the scene but receive no meaningful behavior. The intended later behavior became:
Dispatch accepted → suspect exists → Anyi reaches the scene → scene behavior actually begins.
High-severity ambushes, mass shootouts, officer distress, and similar dangerous scenes can
resist/fight. Pursuit-oriented crimes such as kidnapping, hijacking, vehicle pursuit and
reckless driving can flee. Ordinary criminal scenes should remain wary and interactable rather
than freezing like a mannequin.

Another important correction was surrender timing. Earlier logic could mark a suspect
compliant immediately when a surrender command was issued. The intended two-step behavior
became: first Secure command issues HandsUp and leaves compliance pending; after a short
visible compliance interval, the state becomes genuinely compliant; the next Secure action
can perform the actual arrest/secure transition.

Death handling was also refined. CompleteDispatchOnSuspectDeath was retained as an intended
capability, but the event should not magically disappear merely because an unrelated NPC
killed the suspect while Anyi was still far away. The death completion is tied to the actual
scene/player context.

A separate recurring bug involved Dispatch/Convoy terminal closure. Runtime evidence showed
the prisoner could reach prison and booking could complete, while Dispatch remained active.
The intended correction was to let Convoy completion close the Dispatch that owns that active
transport, remove the yellow/suspect blips, restore the waypoint, start the cooldown, clear
the incident, and make the next Dispatch available.

CRIMINAL ASSET DATABASE AND XML DIRECTION

The project deliberately moved away from hard-coding large amounts of criminal Ped, vehicle,
and weapon data inside individual activity classes. The production history records the need
for a dedicated criminal asset database, ultimately represented by LSPDCRIMINALPROFILE.xml.

The purpose is to provide randomized but controlled Ped models, Ped types, vehicles and
weapons for Dispatch Activity, Crime Activity, and Convoy-related criminal actors. This was
created because hard-coded assets led to repetitive actors, repeated models, asset-loading
failures, and activities becoming stuck when a particular hard-coded asset could not be
generated. The database can also reference Gang MemberPool information where appropriate,
while retaining a separation between Police activity ownership and Gang & Turf ownership.

The principle is simple: XML/database data is the source of configurable criminal assets;
the activity code consumes that data rather than becoming a giant list of hashes.

NPC / CIVILIAN / TRAFFIC RESPONSE HISTORY

LSPDNPCResponse became the local Police civilian and traffic-contact owner. It is intentionally
small and local: one nearby foot pedestrian or one nearby driver, rather than a city-wide
scanner, and it does not own Gang data or create Dispatch incidents by itself.

The interaction system grew into stages covering foot greetings, documents, refusal,
station follow, fleeing, resistance, traffic pulling over, traffic documents, traffic refusal,
traffic fleeing, Backup containment, player arrest, Backup securing, physical escort and
Backup transport.

A particularly important physical-handoff improvement was making the Backup officer the
movement owner during the escort. The cuffed citizen is physically attached to the officer
using a measured world offset, the officer navigates to the rear door, the door opens, the
citizen detaches, and a real rear-seat EnterVehicle task performs the loading. The loading
phase does not restart the escort navigation. This prevents competing tasks from making the
citizen wander or breaking the physical handoff.

The later NPC Backup design also explicitly releases the player's Police activity slot after
the prisoner is physically loaded. The Backup unit may continue its bounded departure in the
background, but it no longer blocks the player from starting the next Police activity. This
became one of the stable behaviors that should not be redesigned casually.

POLICE BACKUP: THE MAJOR EVOLUTION

LSPDBackUp became one of the largest and most heavily debugged parts of the project. Its
documented responsibility is to own the player-requested Police support force. Units stage
away from Anyi, drive to the actual owned target, support the event, stand down, and clean up
only their own spawned Police peds and vehicles. It does not own Dispatch custody, Convoy
transport, Gang actors, or ambient GTA Police.

The current implementation has separate request entry points for Dispatch, Convoy support,
Crime Activity support, NPC support, and Gang support. The same Backup class therefore acts
as a support force while the linked event owner remains responsible for the scene itself.

The current Backup implementation uses an explicit assignment lifecycle with asset preparation,
requested/preparing states, travel, arrival, specialized support, standing down, and cleanup.
Its source contains bounded task-refresh and route-recovery timing, model preparation timeouts,
arrival settling, and specialized NPC/Gang constants. The actual current source also contains
explicit Gang state such as GangRouteLocked, per-officer exit/deployment/target/no-target
tracking, per-officer target dictionaries, and Gang player-protection state.

For ordinary Dispatch, Backup follows the actual Dispatch target and can support scene
containment or a fleeing suspect. For pursuit, it can track the actual suspect vehicle and
perform interception. For Convoy, Backup supplies Police AI support while Convoy retains
custody and transport ownership. For Crime Activity, Backup travels to the Crime scene and
supports it without taking over Crime Activity’s criminal actors. For NPC contacts, Backup
physically contains, escorts, loads, and transports the civilian while the NPC Response owner
retains the civilian's interaction state until the handoff is complete.

THE STABLE NPC BACKUP HANDOFF

The NPC Backup path became one of the clearest stable successes in the project. The intended
flow is: citizen is secured/contained → Backup physically escorts the citizen → rear vehicle
door is reached → door opens → citizen enters the real vehicle → NPC_BACKUP_TRANSPORT_STARTED
is recorded → NPC_BACKUP_PLAYER_SESSION_RELEASED is recorded → the Backup unit leaves the
scene → the player is free to continue Police activity → bounded background cleanup finishes
later.

The current Backup source explicitly separates BlocksPlayerActivities from Active. Once
transport has started and the player's session has been released, the Backup remains active
only for its bounded background departure and no longer owns the player's activity slot.
This behavior is important and should be preserved.

GANG & TURF: FROM OBSERVATION TO ACTIVE GANG INCIDENT

Gang behavior was intentionally kept separate from Universal Dispatch. LSPDGangAdapterResponse
owns the small local Gang/Turf incident layer: it observes a nearby threat, holds the world
state while the threat remains active, and resolves after the threat actually ends. It does
not edit external Gang data, create a Dispatch callout, or delete entities it did not create.

The adapter distinguishes the broader ActiveThreats set from the narrower ActiveCombatThreats
set. ActiveThreats can contain nearby same-faction context. ActiveCombatThreats is intended
to contain confirmed participants in the confrontation. This distinction became important
for Police Backup: nearby Gang members should not automatically become Police targets merely
because they are close to a firefight.

The Gang layer also tracks protected Gang actors. The existing Gang/Turf integration can
identify player-owned/allied actors, including Anyiii-related protected actors. That
protection is used as a narrow safety boundary: Police Backup should not attack protected
Gang actors and can repair a misdirected GTA combat task if necessary.

During active Gang Backup, confirmed combat participants can be held in their confrontation
through a temporary engagement hold. The adapter does not turn every nearby Gang member
hostile; it specifically maintains the actors already confirmed as attackers.

VANILLA GANG BEHAVIOR

LSPDVanillaGangResponse became the layer for recognizing and reacting to vanilla or integrated
Gang behavior before and around Backup. Its historical behavior includes Stealth, Wary and
AttackReady awareness variation. The intention was that not every Gang encounter becomes an
automatic all-out war. Some actors can remain quiet or cautious, while genuinely aggressive
actors can escalate.

A known Anyiii/player-owned actor is treated differently from an ordinary hostile Gang actor.
The project history repeatedly emphasizes that the Gang system is an integration boundary,
not something Police Backup should rewrite. The current code uses GangData definitions,
player-owned/created-by-player status, known Anyiii companion model recognition, and existing
member-pool recognition to distinguish actors.

One unresolved area from the latest testing is instance-level ownership when a shared model
pool contains an ally. A model-hash-only boundary can be insufficient if the same model is
used by both friendly and hostile instances. The user reported a friendly Gang ally being
shot by Police Backup during a Gang fight, but the latest runtime log did not directly record
that exact friendly-fire event. Therefore the event is a user-reported gameplay observation,
not a log-proven event. Any future hardening must use the existing GangData/actor ownership
APIs rather than inventing a new parallel ownership system.

GANG BACKUP: LATEST RUNTIME HISTORY AND CURRENT PROBLEMS

The September 21 runtime session is especially important for the next continuation. The
session around 19:15–19:20 showed a Gang Backup request against Ballas / Anyiii’s Gang. The
system detected a threat with four members and two active combat participants, created two
Backup units with four officers, drove them to the scene, locked their road routes, applied
temporary player protection, requested officer exits, and deployed the officers.

The runtime then showed all four officers selecting the same target handle because that target
was classified as attacking the player. Combat began and the target died. The log then showed
target-dead/no-valid-target conditions and one Backup driver dying. The system recovered a
replacement driver while a living officer remained.

A major problem became visible after combat had effectively ended: repeated
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_FOOT_SUPPORT_REACHED entries continued at changing positions even after
there was no active combat participant. This demonstrates that the Gang foot-support layer
could continue issuing/reaching positioning behavior after the combat phase had lost a valid
target. The intended hard fix is to treat foot support as a transition, not as an endlessly
reissued task, and to stop chasing a stale support coordinate when no valid target exists.

Another directly proven problem occurred during Gang standdown. A Gang unit hit
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_UNIT_RELEASED with Reason=DriverReentryTimeout and the whole Backup
assignment was released while the Gang threat was still active; the final Gang incident
resolution did not occur until later. This proves that driver reentry failure can release the
whole Gang assignment too early. A dead driver must not make a unit with living foot officers
useless during combat, and a temporary driver-reentry failure must not terminate a still-active
Gang incident.

The latest design direction is therefore asynchronous per-officer Gang support. One unit
should be allowed to fight while another is still arriving. Officers should not wait for
every other officer to exit or reach a common support position. Foot movement should be
guidance only until the officer is near the combat area, after which combat task ownership
takes over. Each officer should select and reselect a valid hostile target independently.
When multiple hostiles exist, simple distribution should reduce unnecessary four-officer
piling onto one target. A dead driver should not invalidate living foot officers. When there
is temporarily no target, an officer should hold near the scene rather than repeatedly chase
a stale coordinate.

THE CURRENT GANG BACKUP HARD-FIX DIRECTION

The intended next implementation preserves the existing architecture and focuses only on
behavioral corrections.

The global every-officer-outside and every-officer-reached gates are to be removed from the
Gang support path. Gang units deploy independently. A shared support position may still be
used as a tactical reference, but it must not be a hard formation point. Combat can start for
one officer while another officer is still moving.

Each officer needs an explicit deployed state, target state, and no-target hold state.
Combat target validation must occur immediately before Task.Combat. The validation boundary
must reject the player, Backup officers, protected Gang actors, civilians, unrelated Gang
actors, invalid/dead peds, and any actor not justified by the active Gang scene.

After a target dies, the officer should reselect a valid live hostile target rather than
remain tied to a dead handle. Target priority should favor an actor attacking the player,
then an actor attacking Backup, then a confirmed active combat participant, then another
valid hostile participant within the engagement boundary.

Temporary player protection should remain. If an officer is already attacking a friendly
player-owned Gang actor, the system should clear that task, restore the friendly relationship
and retarget. The protection repair should be logged as a transition rather than every frame.

The Gang response should survive brief zero-participant gaps through a short continuity grace.
The existing adapter already contains a zero-participant hold concept. The goal is to avoid
immediately releasing Backup when the firefight briefly has no confirmed participant but the
same local scene can reengage.

Standdown must be event-owned. A Gang incident that is still active should not be terminated
just because one driver failed to reenter a vehicle. After the Gang incident genuinely ends,
the force can return, leave and release. Gang Backup must never turn into a permanent
companion following Anyi.

TASK OWNERSHIP RULES

The project’s repeated debugging history makes this rule non-negotiable: one ped should not
simultaneously have competing navigation, combat, follow, escort, or loading owners.

During Gang support, a foot officer may have a navigation task while approaching the combat
area, but once combat is assigned, the combat task owns the officer. The support layer must
not keep reissuing a navigation task on top of combat.

During NPC physical escort, the officer owns movement and the citizen is physically attached
to the officer. Once the rear door is reached, the loading task owns the citizen. The system
must not restart the approach after the loading boundary.

During Dispatch vehicle interception, Backup owns its responding officers and the
interception vehicle behavior, while Dispatch continues to own the incident and suspect
identity.

During Convoy, Convoy owns prisoner custody and transport; Backup only supplies bounded Police
support. During Crime Activity, Crime Activity owns criminal actors and the scene; Backup only
supports. During Gang response, Gang/Turf owns Gang actors; Backup only supports the Police
side.

PROFILE, MODEL AND RESPONSE-ASSET HISTORY

A significant earlier problem was the Police response force accidentally using Anyi’s personal
player profile assets. Runtime testing produced situations resembling Venti + PolIgnus being
spawned as response units. The intended separation became explicit:

Player OfficerModel / Player VehicleModel belong to Anyi’s Police profile.
ResponseOfficerModel / ResponseVehicleModel belong to spawned Police response units.

Convoy drivers and Backup response officers use the response-side assets rather than copying
the player's personal profile. The XML profile system was adjusted to carry this separation.

This was another example of the same ownership principle: the player's identity is not the
same object as the world’s responding Police force.

UI / LOGGING HISTORY

Logging became an essential part of the project because many bugs could not be understood
from gameplay alone. The project developed runtime logs, diagnostic logs, event-specific
categories, and explicit lifecycle transitions.

The Anyi Profile startup hub is a related project component. Its history established a compact
Anyi Profile interface with player-model favorites, protagonist switching protection, and an
independent NAudio-based music layer. Its navigation became hierarchical, with Insert as the
master open/close key. Separate normal and diagnostic logs were intended to show boot,
configuration, UI initialization, model changes, music initialization, protection errors,
and UI exceptions.

The Police system follows the same philosophy: logs should identify transitions such as
Backup requested, arrived, officer deployed, target selected, target reselected, friendly
actor rejected, combat started, combat ended, standdown, release, and cleanup. Repeating a
transition every frame is undesirable because it hides the actual event history.

For the next Gang hardening work, useful transition categories include:
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_OFFICER_DEPLOYED_INDEPENDENTLY,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_UNIT_SUPPORT_STARTED,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_TARGET_RESELECTED,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_PROTECTED_ACTOR_REJECTED,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_FRIENDLY_FIRE_REPAIRED,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_NO_TARGET_HOLD,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_DRIVER_LOST_BUT_OFFICER_REMAINS,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_ASSIGNMENT_HELD_FOR_REENGAGEMENT,
POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_REENGAGED,
and POLICE_BACKUP_GANG_ASSIGNMENT_RELEASED.

AUGUST 2026: MIXED-REVISION AND CLEAN-ROOM LESSONS

August production repeatedly exposed mixed-revision failures. One documented example showed
a source package that was described as an 8:00 PM baseline, while a later build contained
SET_VEHICLE_HALT, World.IsWaypointActive and obsolete FightAgainst() problems that were not
actually present in the baseline. The diagnosis was not that 35 independent bugs had suddenly
appeared. The files belonged to different revisions and their contracts had drifted apart.

Another example involved a newer NPC file expecting seven new configuration properties while
the installed Police Config remained the older version. That produced a CS1061 cascade. The
correct response was synchronization of the directly dependent files, not replacing the
whole project.

The production history therefore established a clean-room rule: use a known-good stable
Visual Studio project, rebuild it, deploy the resulting DLL, and avoid copying individual
files from an experimental project into the stable project unless their dependency contract
has been checked.

The project also explicitly adopted the SOURCE → LOG → GAMEPLAY debugging triangle. Source
shows what actually exists. Runtime logs show what actually executed. Gameplay observation
shows what the player actually experienced. A giant historical chat is useful context but
must not be treated as proof that a proposed change was implemented.

THE RAW-NATIVE CRASH LESSON

A later crash investigation found a concrete fatal ScriptHookV native issue in an
experimental Police NPC source revision. The uploaded source contained a raw native call
using 0x4C9BF537BE263FD4 in a method checking whether a Police siren was active. The runtime
fatal error was “Can't find native 0x4C9BF537BE263FD4”. The production history correctly
treated this as a smoking gun rather than a vague suspicion.

The lesson is permanent: never invent or guess a raw native hash. A managed try/catch does
not make an invalid ScriptHookV native safe. Native availability must be established from
the correct Enhanced runtime/native reference before use.

SHVDN / GTA V ENHANCED BASELINE

The current project targets GTA V Enhanced on Steam. The deployed scripts directory is the
real GTA V Enhanced scripts folder. The project uses ScriptHookV and ScriptHookVDotNet
Enhanced 3.9.0.6, with Enhanced runtime/API 1.1.0.6 and Target API 3. Visual Studio 2022
Community is used for the C# project with Debug x64. References include the Enhanced
ScriptHookVDotNet3.dll and LemonUI.SHVDN3.dll where required.

The known ASI/plugin environment has included ScriptHookV, ScriptHookVDotNet Enhanced,
Menyoo.asi, OpenRPF.asi, PackfileLimitAdjusterEnhanced.asi, ModkitLimitAdjusterEnhanced.asi,
DirectStorageFix.asi, DecalPatch.asi, and Dynamic Population Density.asi.

The project’s managed scripts include ChaosResponse.dll, AnyiCrimePartner.dll,
AnyiRealisticRoadReaction.dll, Dismemberment.dll, DriverJobs.dll, GangAndTurfMod.dll,
iFruitAddon2.dll, LivingLSAIs.dll and PersistencePro.dll, alongside the Police Authority
system. Unrelated systems must not be casually changed while debugging a Police-specific issue.

THE RELATED ANYI PARTNER PROJECT

The Anyi Partner project is related context but is not the owner of the Police Authority
system. Its history involved companion state, passenger/follow behavior, combat ownership,
weapon profiles, Menyoo XML structure, selected-character UI, and convoy behavior.

The same task-ownership lesson appeared there. Follow maintenance could overwrite combat,
weapon profiles could be repeatedly reapplied, explosive mode could replace the intended
weapon, and the Menyoo XML structure could disagree with the newer C# loader. A native
convoy layer was added so companions could use separate cars or motorcycles and follow
Anyi's vehicle. A second companion could occupy an escort vehicle as a passenger shooter
when possible.

This project should remain separate from LSPD Police ownership unless a specific integration
has already been documented.

THE ANYI PROFILE STARTUP HUB

The Anyi Profile UI evolved into a startup customization hub rather than a general Ped
spawner. Favorite models are player-model presets: selecting a favorite changes Anyi’s
existing player rather than spawning a separate Ped. Protagonist switching protection can
remain BLOCKED by default and can be temporarily allowed when desired.

The intended compact hierarchy is:

ANYI PROFILE
Protagonist Switching: BLOCKED
Favorite Player Models
Elf Radio
Refresh Music Library
Close

Favorite Models and Elf Radio use nested navigation, and Backspace returns to the parent menu
instead of closing the whole UI. Insert is the master open/close key.

The music system uses NAudio as a separate audio stream rather than GTA’s internal Self Radio
station system. This was intentionally kept separate from the Police project’s gameplay
ownership.

SEPTEMBER 2026: DATABASE, UI AND GAMEPLAY REVIEW

By September, the project had become substantially more modular. The gameplay review
documentation emphasized Police vehicle controls, radio, GPS, contextual UI, consistent
controller controls, Gang & Turf read-only recognition, friendly Anyiii Gang members,
hostile Gang incidents, vanilla Gang recognition, scene aftermath, cleanup, and a clean
return to normal GTA.

The review also explicitly removed or deferred several older concepts. Chaos Response was
no longer supposed to own the Police crime system or Police dispatch audio. Evidence markers
were out. Citizen Mode and Gang Leader Mode were deferred. Police Mode stabilization became
the priority.

The same review identified the criminal database problem: Dispatch, Crime Activity and
Convoy request activity needed randomized criminal assets from LSPDCRIMINALPROFILE.xml
rather than hard-coded Ped, vehicle and weapon combinations. The database already existed
and needed to be treated as the activity asset source.

The September review also identified usability problems: entering Police Mode could still
present redundant “open Police Authority” steps; Patrol should immediately start the Police
activity state; repeated Y presses while the main Police UI was open could become annoying
until the menu was explicitly closed. The desired direction was direct gameplay access and
clean input ownership.

WHAT IS CURRENTLY KNOWN-GOOD / SHOULD NOT BE REDESIGNED

The project has several behaviors that were explicitly working and should be treated as
protected baselines unless a new bug directly requires a change.

The physical NPC Backup handoff is one. The player can request Backup, the unit physically
contains the citizen, escorts them to the rear door, loads them, starts transport, releases
the player's session, and leaves in the background.

The Backup Dispatch vehicle branch has also worked: it can track the actual suspect vehicle,
pursue/intercept, contain, make the suspect exit, have officers dismount, obtain compliance,
let the player perform the final arrest, and then pass the prisoner into Convoy physical
custody and station transport.

Full Convoy station handoff has worked. The physical custody stages include
EscortApproach, SecuringContact, Escorting, VehicleDoorApproach, VehicleDoorReached,
DoorOpened, Loading, and Loaded. Real GTA tasks are used for escort/loading rather than
faking a prisoner teleport.

Gang Backup route locking is already conceptually established: once a Gang unit reaches
its road node, the route is locked so the generic route-recovery loop does not retarget the
vehicle while its officers support the firefight.

The project also intentionally suppresses normal wanted-level escalation during Police
Authority Gang incidents according to the Authority layer. That responsibility should stay
with Authority rather than being moved into Backup.

### What I am fixing in this revision

The biggest one is the suspect lifecycle.

Right now your game can create a dispatch-owned suspect, but ordinary crime types such as suspicious gang activity, arms dealing, kidnapping, etc. can arrive at the scene with the ped doing basically nothing because the old `EnsureSceneSubject()` creates the ped, marks `BlockPermanentEvents = true`, and doesn't necessarily give it an actual behavior until certain event types qualify. That's exactly why you're seeing your "statue suspect." The current Core source confirms that scene subjects are spawned separately and only certain types/severity get an immediate combat/flee task. fileciteturn57file13

The new behavior is:

`Dispatch accepted → suspect exists → Anyi reaches scene → scene behavior actually starts`

Gang ambush / mass shootout / officer distress / high severity → **resist and fight**

Ped pursuit / kidnapping / hijacking / vehicle pursuit / reckless driver → **flee**

Normal criminal scene → **stay wary, look at Anyi, remain interactable**, not freeze forever.

That means the suspect isn't going to run away before you even arrive, but he also isn't going to stand there like an NPC mannequin after you arrive.

### The surrender bug is being properly fixed

Your runtime repeatedly says:

> `Order the suspect to show hands and reach a compliant state first.`

and then you never get the actual hands-up progression. fileciteturn57file3turn57file19

The old logic was declaring `SuspectCompliant` too eagerly when the surrender command was issued.

I changed that into a real two-step process:

**First Secure press:**  
Police command → suspect receives `HandsUp()` → state remains pending → notification says wait.

**After ~1.5 seconds:**  
If the suspect is still alive, not shooting and not fighting → state becomes `SuspectCompliant` → actual hands-up notification.

**Second Secure press:**  
Now the suspect is actually arrested/secured.

So the gameplay should finally feel like:

> "Show me your hands."

then

> *suspect actually puts hands up*

then

> "You're under arrest."

rather than the mod pretending a hands-up task happened instantaneously.

The current source already had the concept of `SurrenderRequested`; I tightened the transition so the first press doesn't lie about the suspect already being compliant.

### Death is no longer allowed to magically finish the job from across the city

I kept your `CompleteDispatchOnSuspectDeath=True`, because you explicitly want a resisting suspect that you neutralize to be able to finish the event.

But it now depends on being **at the scene**.

So:

`Suspect dies while Anyi is nearby` → dispatch can close successfully.

`Suspect gets killed by a random gang or another NPC while Anyi is still driving there` → dispatch does **not** magically disappear.

This is especially important because you've had gangs interfering with your scenes and wondered whether *they* killed the suspect.

Your runtime already shows the Police system can detect gang attacks such as Santos Vagos attacking Police Authority Anyi, and the dispatch system correctly reaches `Offered → Accepted → EnRoute`. fileciteturn57file14turn57file15

Your current runtime showed response units being created with the same model hashes as your personal player profile. The previous response code used the current profile's vehicle/model for response units, which meant your Police world could become:

The new profile structure separates:

Your old runtime showed the convoy getting into a horrible repeating condition where the prisoner entity was lost and the watchdog just kept reporting the same error over and over.

The LSPD project is specifically intended as an immersive, personal Anyi police-roleplay system rather than a total-conversion game. The LSPD idea has three genuinely different gameplay states. Police Officer Anyi should be a genuine police-authority mode. While on duty, ordinary vanilla law-enforcement should not treat the player as a criminal, and Anyi should not receive ordinary wanted stars merely for being a police officer. The police-authority state should be local to the player and should not globally rewrite the maximum wanted level or permanently destroy all police behavior in the game. Police Officer mode should create its own dispatch, patrol, scene investigation, arrest, transport and officer-interaction layer. The Gang Anyi Territories or Superb Anyi's Gang must be different from Police Authority Mode..

The Police Officer mode should support selectable department/agency, selectable station/interior, selectable officer ped, selectable custom ped model name, selectable police vehicle model name, police profile customization, LSPD/Sheriff/NOOSE/FIB style agency configuration if desired, and configuration through XML/INI rather than hardcoded values. Anyi specifically likes the idea of using his custom polignus vehicle as a police pursuit vehicle. It is treated as a user-provided/custom vehicle model, not assumed to be a verified vanilla GTA police asset. The giant hollow red block that appeared on screen when using the PolIgnus siren is a known gameplay/asset problem. The police logic must not “fix” this by randomly changing native siren parameters or introducing unsupported wrappers. The correct approach is to isolate PolIgnus profile behavior, validate the model, allow emergency lights separately from native siren, and permit NativeSiren=false by configuration until the custom asset’s siren/light setup is explicitly verified. Standard vanilla models such as police, police2, police3, policet and similar verified models remain useful for baseline testing. The first stable test should normally use a known vanilla police vehicle and a known vanilla police ped; PolIgnus can then be enabled as an asset-specific profile once the core is stable.

Do not blindly install IPL/YMAP/MLO data or force Online interiors just because they exist on a wiki. Do not invent interior names or coordinates. Anything that is not verified in Anyi’s build should be explicitly marked “requires in-game verification” and treated as an exterior-safe option rather than a forced interior.

The police UI is intended to use LemonUI.SHVDN3. Anyi wants something more immersive than a trainer menu. It should include an interaction menu with Duty/Profile, Dispatch/Radio, Station/Interior, Vehicle, Evidence/Inventory, Interaction, Settings and quick GPS. The exact keys can be configurable in the INI, with a proven rising-edge physical-key implementation rather than legacy KeyDown toggles. The menu should be context-sensitive. When no call exists, the Dispatch menu should show availability. When a dispatch is offered, it should present accept/reject. When an incident is active, it should show context-appropriate actions such as approach/investigate, secure suspect, request transport, cancel dispatch, follow convoy, cancel convoy and deliver prisoner. Vehicle menu functionality should support emergency lights, siren mode, doors, radio and radio-station control. Evidence menu should support placing and removing cosmetic evidence markers. The dispatch system is one of the most important requested features. Anyi wants a real dispatch/callout concept rather than a random mission circle. A dispatch should be offered to the player while on duty, with a bottom-left notification and optionally a minimap blip. It should never use a rigid mission timer. Anyi can be AFK, drive slowly, investigate elsewhere or reject the call. The call has a realistic cooldown after completion or rejection, but the mission itself has no deadline. The player accepts or rejects the call through a configurable key or menu. Accepting should mark the call active and assign a waypoint. The suspect or incident should not disappear simply because Anyi takes time to reach the scene. The call must have explicit lifecycle states such as Offered, Accepted/Active, EnRoute, OnScene, Investigating, SuspectFleeing, SuspectCompliant, SuspectResisting, Arrested, AwaitingTransport, Escorting, Completed, Cancelled, Failed or Compromised. A cancelled dispatch should remove its blip and clean up only entities that the dispatch itself owns. A failed dispatch should have an explicit reason such as suspect deceased, scene invalid, transport destroyed or subject genuinely missing. The previous implementation had a specific bug because organic events were sometimes created directly as Active even though the UI’s acceptance flow expected Offered; this must never happen again. A scene that has an actual fleeing suspect should change to SuspectFleeing rather than simply “subject unavailable.” A dead suspect can become a homicide/investigation scene instead of disappearing. The system should create actual world behavior first and only then promote it to a dispatch where practical: actual vehicle theft, actual reckless driving, actual pedestrian fleeing, actual gang gathering, actual gunfire, actual violent disturbance, etc. It should not simply choose an arbitrary nearby civilian and label him “PedFleeing” without making that person flee.

The requested callout/event variety includes gang pursuits, kidnapping pursuits, vehicle chases, pedestrian pursuits, random criminal meetings, organization activity, vehicle theft or kidnapping, reckless drivers, street disturbances, suspicious meetings, officers responding to incidents, traffic stops and other natural police events. Events should be sparse and contextual rather than constantly appearing. Anyi wants realistic cooldowns, not mission timers. The mod should not generate a new event every few seconds or constantly scan the entire city. A patrol officer should occasionally discover an event while driving or observing the world. Some events may already involve existing GTA entities; others can use managed spawned entities, but if the system spawns a suspect, witness or victim it must explicitly own those entities and maintain them until the incident is completed, cancelled or safely cleaned up.

Police response needs to feel like a real response rather than magic teleportation. Each responding unit should have a patrol origin or station origin, current position, destination, role, current task, call assignment and arrival state. A dispatch should find the nearest suitable available patrol unit or create a new response unit only if capacity allows. The unit should actually drive to the scene. If a suspect already exists, that must not prevent the response vehicle from receiving its drive-to-scene task. A previously observed bug was that response units could be spawned when a subject already existed but were not always commanded to drive, leaving them standing still. This must be corrected in the final implementation. Patrol units should return to patrol after an incident instead of accumulating or vanishing arbitrarily. A unit created by a dispatch should be cleaned up or returned to patrol after the incident ends according to configuration. Normal Anyi mode must not leave custom LSPD units active after exiting police mode; police-owned entities must be cleaned cleanly on mode transition or reset.

Police Officer authority must be explicit. A dedicated authority state should distinguish IsPoliceOfficer, IsGangAuthority, PoliceHostilityDisabled, VanillaWantedPolicy and CustomCrimeLevel. Police Officer mode should establish a protected-authority state so nearby ordinary police do not attack An

yi. The previous code was too blunt because it repeatedly did SET_PLAYER_WANTED_LEVEL = 0, SET_POLICE_IGNORE_PLAYER = true and SET_LAW_PEDS_CAN_ATTACK_NON_WANTED_PLAYER_THIS_FRAME = false every authority refresh, and that approach destroyed too much of GTA’s normal police behavior. The new design must localize the effect to the player’s authority state and ensure police stop targeting Anyi while he is on duty without globally rewriting the world. Normal mode should restore vanilla law enforcement behavior. Gang mode should not permanently disable wanted levels. When Anyi commits actual chaos in Gang mode, wanted levels or a custom equivalent escalation can rise and police can respond intelligently. When Anyi leaves Gang mode, the custom system should cleanly restore the ordinary GTA behavior without leaving permanently modified relationships or dispatch states behind.

Police NPC interaction must feel natural and stateful. The desired state model is something like Normal → Aware → Wary → Approaching → Interacting → Compliant/Resisting/Fleeing/Completed, rather than simply scanning peds every few seconds and repeatedly issuing look or cower tasks. A civilian near Anyi as a police officer can look toward him, move aside, become wary, cower under nearby gunfire, approach for help or provide information/papers in a specific interaction. A police officer encountering an armed Anyi on duty should be able to observe and approach rather than instantly attack him. If Anyi carries a knife or ordinary pistol in normal gameplay, nearby police may watch him, approach, ask him to lower the weapon or investigate. A traffic stop should allow Anyi to approach the driver, attempt to communicate, request documents/papers or identify suspicious behavior. If the driver refuses to stop, the event can escalate into a pursuit. NPCs should not slam their cars into Anyi simply because the script is attempting an interaction. The system needs interaction states, cooldowns and proper stop/approach tasks. The previous implementation was too repetitive and aggressively checked NPCs every scan, producing robotic behavior and repeated “civilian acknowledges Officer Anyi” logs. Persistent per-entity state must prevent duplicate interactions and repeated task issuance.

Arrest behavior must be explicit. A resisting suspect should be able to flee or fight and continue being pursued. A compliant suspect should surrender rather than immediately become “arrested” merely because Anyi pressed one key. The desired visuals include hands-up/cowering behavior, surrender posture, and secured-arrest state with hands behind the back/handcuffed. The interaction should allow Anyi to secure a compliant suspect and then initiate prisoner transport. A suspect who resists and is incapacitated can be treated differently from a suspect who voluntarily surrenders. The callout should not be marked successfully completed simply because the player shot the suspect; the system should decide the outcome based on the incident type and the suspect’s final state. A dead suspect can create an investigation scene rather than an automatic success. An arrested suspect should be explicitly tracked by the custody/convoy system.

The prison convoy is a major requested system and has already failed badly in earlier builds. The proper architecture is a real prisoner-custody state machine: Arrested → Secured → AwaitingTransport → LoadedIntoTransport → Transporting → PrisonArrival → BookIn → Released/Completed. The prisoner must be owned by the convoy manager while transported. The transport vehicle, driver and escort units must be owned by the convoy manager. The prisoner should remain handcuffed and assigned to the transport seat throughout Transporting. Every few seconds, a custody watchdog can verify the prisoner still exists, is still alive, is still in the assigned transport and has not accidentally exited. If GTA somehow ejects or dislodges the prisoner, the system should attempt controlled re-seating. The prisoner should not casually walk out of the convoy van. The prisoner may be intentionally dismounted only at the prison/holding destination or during a configured emergency/compromised state. If the transport vehicle is destroyed, the state should become TransportCompromised and offer recovery rather than leaving a blue marker forever. The convoy should not teleport vehicles beside Anyi and then rely on them to magically escort. The convoy manager should issue driver/escort tasks, maintain spacing without constantly reissuing tasks, and know its destination. The player should be able to cancel the convoy. The prisoner should be booked at the station or prison, and only then should the dispatch/convoy be considered completed. The user has specifically complained that previous convoys stood still, escorts ran away or became robotic, the criminal died, the blue circle remained, the prison was locked, no completion message appeared and the criminal could leave the transport van. All of those are first-class bugs to prevent in the new architecture.

Evidence markers are intended to be cosmetic and immersive, similar to the LSPDFR evidence-marker concept. They can be placed on the ground and removed by interaction. The default model may be configured via XML. Evidence markers should not affect core gameplay unless a future evidence system explicitly adds that. The code must keep the evidence record type in a coherent ownership boundary, preferably in the Evidence subsystem rather than as a mysterious nested type that another source file assumes. The previous implementation suffered from an EvidenceMarkerRecord mismatch between AnyiLSPDEvidence.cs and AnyiLSPDPoliceCore.cs; future files must use one synchronized type definition.

Voice is another intended subsystem. The previous implementation dynamically looked for System.Speech and fell back to subtitles because the assembly was unavailable. That fallback is acceptable during development, but the dispatcher should only speak meaningful radio events. Desired examples include “Unit Anyi, disturbance reported nearby”, “Suspect fleeing on foot”, “Prisoner transport is en route”, and “Unit Anyi, proceed to Mission Row for prisoner transfer.” Voice should not be spammed every tick. If the TTS dependency is unavailable, the script should continue normally with subtitles without crashes.

The police map/icon requirement is explicit. The selected station should have an LSPD icon on the map, and Quick GPS should be able to set waypoints to the nearest police station, prison/jail drop-off, fire station, medical center or another configured point where such points exist. The map/blip logic must have cleanup and should not leave stale blue circles after a cancelled or completed dispatch. Only the currently active incident should own its incident blip. The mod should support police departments/agencies such as LSPD, LSSD, NOOSE and FIB through profiles, but these should be configuration choices, not hardwired behaviors. Officer ped models and vehicle models should be configurable, including arbitrary addon ped/vehicle names provided by Anyi. INI should contain runtime tuning and keybinds. Station XML should contain locations, headings, interior mode and optional interior coordinates. The user wants the ability to type or change a model name for a custom addon police ped or a custom police vehicle like PolIgnus without recompiling the whole script.

The police vehicle menu should include lights, doors, emergency signals, radio and radio station. The system should not assume every police vehicle has the same door count or the same siren behavior. The previous build hit an API mismatch with VehicleDoorIndex; future door functions must use the exact enum/index type exposed by the installed SHVDN Enhanced API and must not invent an int overload. The vehicle emergency system also previously suffered from a mismatch in ConfigureEmergencyMode(...) signatures. The project’s XML/INI architecture should be simple enough for Anyi to understand and edit. The project should not require dozens of external packages or dependencies just to compile. A single AnyiLSPDImmersive.dll is preferred for the core system. Separate DLLs should exist only when there is a genuinely independent subsystem, such as an optional Gang adapter. Multiple .cs files are encouraged for separation of responsibilities but should normally compile into one main DLL. The user explicitly does not want the assistant to create an entire Visual Studio project package; the user wants to create the project himself, add references, then copy or add the individual C# files. The assistant should provide coherent sets of source files from the same revision. Never hand the user a Core from one revision and a World/Evidence/Config file from another revision that expects incompatible signatures.

The major historical development lesson from the previous LSPD iterations is that adding every feature at once made the project unplayable and caused repeated compiler mismatches. Anyi now explicitly wants the assistant to build the project one feature at a time. A new feature must compile before the next one is added. If a feature requires changing several source files, all related files must be provided as one synchronized feature patch. The assistant must account for every changed parameter, field, XML element and parser mapping. If C# produces a warning such as “parameter is unused,” the assistant should decide whether it is an intentional harmless warning, a sign of unfinished logic, or something that should be removed; the user does not want to be told to ignore endless warnings that come from sloppy implementation. The distinction is important: build-blocking errors must be fixed; intentional warnings should be minimized; IDE suggestions are not blockers.

The first milestone for a rebuilt Anyi LSPD system should therefore be deliberately small and stable. It should establish a project that compiles cleanly, loads into GTA, supports Normal Anyi, supports entering/exiting Police Officer mode, establishes local police authority correctly, ensures nearby ordinary police do not attack a legitimate officer, spawns at most one or a very small controlled number of patrol units, supports one configurable police ped and one configurable police vehicle, and maintains a clean mode reset. The first dispatch should then be added as a standalone feature, with accept/reject/cancel, one persistent suspect, proper scene lifecycle, real drive-to-scene behavior and no mission timer. Only after that works should prisoner arrest and transport be added. Then NPC interactions. Then organic events. Then Gang Anyi escalation. Then tactical response. Then military. Then richer interiors and additional callouts. Evidence, voice and optional gang adapter can be introduced at the appropriate feature milestone rather than all at once.

The current project experienced a series of compile errors that should be remembered as examples of what not to repeat. These included missing PatrolPedModel, missing CalloutMinDistance/CalloutMaxDistance, List<string>.Length instead of .Count, undefined ground, VehicleDoorIndex vs int mismatches, float-to-int conversions, VehicleDrivingFlags.Normal being unavailable, Hash.TASK_FLEE_PED being unavailable, Hash.IS_PED_COP

These are concrete reminders to verify all members against the actual current references and keep classes synchronized. The recent compilation cycle finally reduced some error counts, but then runtime testing still showed the architecture was unplayable. Do not return to those old patterns.

The runtime logs from the previous LSPD build exposed the most important behavioral failures. The mod successfully loaded GangData, MemberPool and TurfZoneData, so the data connector can work. It could create police vehicles and officers, but it sometimes spawned patrols too frequently and left units active when the player returned to Normal mode. It created organic events and dispatches but sometimes immediately accepted them even when they were intended to be Offered. It could report CALL_FAILED | SubjectUnavailable because the suspect entity was not robustly owned/persisted. It sometimes spawned response units but did not reliably give them drive-to-scene tasks when a subject already existed. It repeatedly logged civilian acknowledgement without remembering that the same pedestrian had already been processed. Gang Anyi could trigger custom response too aggressively, sometimes producing a severity 5 response and SWAT immediately instead of the intended gradual escalation. Voice often fell back because System.Speech was unavailable. The reset function could clean units, but simply switching to Normal did not always clean them. These behaviors demonstrate why the next build must be stateful and ownership-driven.

The current police interaction philosophy should be “natural world simulation” rather than “mission manager.” A civilian should not suddenly freeze or become a task dummy because Anyi walked near them. A police officer should not attack Anyi because the mod failed to synchronize authority with vanilla police logic. A traffic offender should not ram Anyi merely because the AI task was constantly reissued. A suspect should not disappear because Anyi took thirty seconds to arrive. A prison convoy should not exist only as a set of spawned vehicles; it should be a persistent stateful operation. A dispatch marker should disappear when cancelled and a scene should remain coherent until its final state. A patrol officer should not repeatedly react to the same pedestrian or scan the same gang member every second.
