The LSPD project is specifically intended as an immersive, personal Anyi police-roleplay system rather than a total-conversion game. Anyi is not trying to replace GTA V Enhanced or create a completely separate game. He wants a personal police-simulation layer inside his existing Enhanced sandbox, similar in spirit to the roleplay features that players might associate with LSPDFR, but implemented for his own GTA V Enhanced environment through C#, LemonUI, XML/INI and selected external data connectors. He has explicitly said he does not want to make a “different game” from GTA V Enhanced. The goal is to make his own personal mod for ordinary police dispatches, patrols, realistic police response, Gang Anyi behavior, custom ped/vehicle profiles, vanilla or safely verified interiors, evidence, prisoner transport, police interaction and contextual world response.

The LSPD idea has three genuinely different gameplay states. Police Officer Anyi should be a genuine police-authority mode. While on duty, ordinary vanilla law-enforcement should not treat the player as a criminal, and Anyi should not receive ordinary wanted stars merely for being a police officer. The police-authority state should be local to the player and should not globally rewrite the maximum wanted level or permanently destroy all police behavior in the game. Police Officer mode should create its own dispatch, patrol, scene investigation, arrest, transport and officer-interaction layer. The Gang Anyi Territories or Superb Anyi's Gang must be different from Police Authority Mode..

The Police Officer mode should support selectable department/agency, selectable station/interior, selectable officer ped, selectable custom ped model name, selectable police vehicle model name, police profile customization, LSPD/Sheriff/NOOSE/FIB style agency configuration if desired, and configuration through XML/INI rather than hardcoded values. Anyi specifically likes the idea of using his custom polignus vehicle as a police pursuit vehicle. It is treated as a user-provided/custom vehicle model, not assumed to be a verified vanilla GTA police asset. The giant hollow red block that appeared on screen when using the PolIgnus siren is a known gameplay/asset problem. The police logic must not “fix” this by randomly changing native siren parameters or introducing unsupported wrappers. The correct approach is to isolate PolIgnus profile behavior, validate the model, allow emergency lights separately from native siren, and permit NativeSiren=false by configuration until the custom asset’s siren/light setup is explicitly verified. Standard vanilla models such as police, police2, police3, policet and similar verified models remain useful for baseline testing. The first stable test should normally use a known vanilla police vehicle and a known vanilla police ped; PolIgnus can then be enabled as an asset-specific profile once the core is stable.

The police station/interior system should be safe. Anyi wants accessible LSPD locations and interiors from Story Mode and, where safe, Online/DLC content as well, but he explicitly wants research and verification before forcing any interior into the game because he wants to avoid DLC or interior void falling ped  crashes. The current configuration has used Mission Row as the safest primary verified vanilla LSPD interior while other stations may be exterior-safe anchors until their interiors are verified in his exact Enhanced build. Future interior support should be data-driven, with a station registry containing exterior position, heading, interior mode, interior identifier when genuinely verified, optional entry/exit points and NPC placement. Do not blindly install IPL/YMAP/MLO data or force Online interiors just because they exist on a wiki. Do not invent interior names or coordinates. Anything that is not verified in Anyi’s build should be explicitly marked “requires in-game verification” and treated as an exterior-safe option rather than a forced interior.

The police UI is intended to use LemonUI.SHVDN3. Anyi wants something more immersive than a trainer menu. It should include an interaction menu with Duty/Profile, Dispatch/Radio, Station/Interior, Vehicle, Evidence/Inventory, Interaction, Settings and quick GPS. The exact keys can be configurable in the INI, with a proven rising-edge physical-key implementation rather than legacy KeyDown toggles. The menu should be context-sensitive. When no call exists, the Dispatch menu should show availability. When a dispatch is offered, it should present accept/reject. When an incident is active, it should show context-appropriate actions such as approach/investigate, secure suspect, request transport, cancel dispatch, follow convoy, cancel convoy and deliver prisoner. Vehicle menu functionality should support emergency lights, siren mode, doors, radio and radio-station control. Evidence menu should support placing and removing cosmetic evidence markers. Settings should control agency, officer model, vehicle model, station/spawn location, owned apartment if relevant, response settings, police profile and key bindings.

The dispatch system is one of the most important requested features. Anyi wants a real dispatch/callout concept rather than a random mission circle. A dispatch should be offered to the player while on duty, with a bottom-left notification and optionally a minimap blip. It should never use a rigid mission timer. Anyi can be AFK, drive slowly, investigate elsewhere or reject the call. The call has a realistic cooldown after completion or rejection, but the mission itself has no deadline. The player accepts or rejects the call through a configurable key or menu. Accepting should mark the call active and assign a waypoint. The suspect or incident should not disappear simply because Anyi takes time to reach the scene. The call must have explicit lifecycle states such as Offered, Accepted/Active, EnRoute, OnScene, Investigating, SuspectFleeing, SuspectCompliant, SuspectResisting, Arrested, AwaitingTransport, Escorting, Completed, Cancelled, Failed or Compromised. A cancelled dispatch should remove its blip and clean up only entities that the dispatch itself owns. A failed dispatch should have an explicit reason such as suspect deceased, scene invalid, transport destroyed or subject genuinely missing. The previous implementation had a specific bug because organic events were sometimes created directly as Active even though the UI’s acceptance flow expected Offered; this must never happen again. A scene that has an actual fleeing suspect should change to SuspectFleeing rather than simply “subject unavailable.” A dead suspect can become a homicide/investigation scene instead of disappearing. The system should create actual world behavior first and only then promote it to a dispatch where practical: actual vehicle theft, actual reckless driving, actual pedestrian fleeing, actual gang gathering, actual gunfire, actual violent disturbance, etc. It should not simply choose an arbitrary nearby civilian and label him “PedFleeing” without making that person flee.

The requested callout/event variety includes gang pursuits, kidnapping pursuits, vehicle chases, pedestrian pursuits, random criminal meetings, organization activity, vehicle theft or kidnapping, reckless drivers, street disturbances, suspicious meetings, officers responding to incidents, traffic stops and other natural police events. Events should be sparse and contextual rather than constantly appearing. Anyi wants realistic cooldowns, not mission timers. The mod should not generate a new event every few seconds or constantly scan the entire city. A patrol officer should occasionally discover an event while driving or observing the world. Some events may already involve existing GTA entities; others can use managed spawned entities, but if the system spawns a suspect, witness or victim it must explicitly own those entities and maintain them until the incident is completed, cancelled or safely cleaned up.

Police response needs to feel like a real response rather than magic teleportation. Each responding unit should have a patrol origin or station origin, current position, destination, role, current task, call assignment and arrival state. A dispatch should find the nearest suitable available patrol unit or create a new response uni

t only if capacity allows. The unit should actually drive to the scene. If a suspect already exists, that must not prevent the response vehicle from receiving its drive-to-scene task. A previously observed bug was that response units could be spawned when a subject already existed but were not always commanded to drive, leaving them standing still. This must be corrected in the final implementation. Patrol units should return to patrol after an incident instead of accumulating or vanishing arbitrarily. A unit created by a dispatch should be cleaned up or returned to patrol after the incident ends according to configuration. Normal Anyi mode must not leave custom LSPD units active after exiting police mode; police-owned entities must be cleaned cleanly on mode transition or reset.

Police Officer authority must be explicit. A dedicated authority state should distinguish IsPoliceOfficer, IsGangAuthority, PoliceHostilityDisabled, VanillaWantedPolicy and CustomCrimeLevel. Police Officer mode should establish a protected-authority state so nearby ordinary police do not attack Anyi. The previous code was too blunt because it repeatedly did SET_PLAYER_WANTED_LEVEL = 0, SET_POLICE_IGNORE_PLAYER = true and SET_LAW_PEDS_CAN_ATTACK_NON_WANTED_PLAYER_THIS_FRAME = false every authority refresh, and that approach destroyed too much of GTA’s normal police behavior. The new design must localize the effect to the player’s authority state and ensure police stop targeting Anyi while he is on duty without globally rewriting the world. Normal mode should restore vanilla law enforcement behavior. Gang mode should not permanently disable wanted levels. When Anyi commits actual chaos in Gang mode, wanted levels or a custom equivalent escalation can rise and police can respond intelligently. When Anyi leaves Gang mode, the custom system should cleanly restore the ordinary GTA behavior without leaving permanently modified relationships or dispatch states behind.

Police NPC interaction must feel natural and stateful. The desired state model is something like Normal → Aware → Wary → Approaching → Interacting → Compliant/Resisting/Fleeing/Completed, rather than simply scanning peds every few seconds and repeatedly issuing look or cower tasks. A civilian near Anyi as a police officer can look toward him, move aside, become wary, cower under nearby gunfire, approach for help or provide information/papers in a specific interaction. A police officer encountering an armed Anyi on duty should be able to observe and approach rather than instantly attack him. If Anyi carries a knife or ordinary pistol in normal gameplay, nearby police may watch him, approach, ask him to lower the weapon or investigate. A traffic stop should allow Anyi to approach the driver, attempt to communicate, request documents/papers or identify suspicious behavior. If the driver refuses to stop, the event can escalate into a pursuit. NPCs should not slam their cars into Anyi simply because the script is attempting an interaction. The system needs interaction states, cooldowns and proper stop/approach tasks. The previous implementation was too repetitive and aggressively checked NPCs every scan, producing robotic behavior and repeated “civilian acknowledges Officer Anyi” logs. Persistent per-entity state must prevent duplicate interactions and repeated task issuance.

Arrest behavior must be explicit. A resisting suspect should be able to flee or fight and continue being pursued. A compliant suspect should surrender rather than immediately become “arrested” merely because Anyi pressed one key. The desired visuals include hands-up/cowering behavior, surrender posture, and secured-arrest state with hands behind the back/handcuffed. The interaction should allow Anyi to secure a compliant suspect and then initiate prisoner transport. A suspect who resists and is incapacitated can be treated differently from a suspect who voluntarily surrenders. The callout should not be marked successfully completed simply because the player shot the suspect; the system should decide the outcome based on the incident type and the suspect’s final state. A dead suspect can create an investigation scene rather than an automatic success. An arrested suspect should be explicitly tracked by the custody/convoy system.

The prison convoy is a major requested system and has already failed badly in earlier builds. The proper architecture is a real prisoner-custody state machine: Arrested → Secured → AwaitingTransport → LoadedIntoTransport → Transporting → PrisonArrival → BookIn → Released/Completed. The prisoner must be owned by the convoy manager while transported. The transport vehicle, driver and escort units must be owned by the convoy manager. The prisoner should remain handcuffed and assigned to the transport seat throughout Transporting. Every few seconds, a custody watchdog can verify the prisoner still exists, is still alive, is still in the assigned transport and has not accidentally exited. If GTA somehow ejects or dislodges the prisoner, the system should attempt controlled re-seating. The prisoner should not casually walk out of the convoy van. The prisoner may be intentionally dismounted only at the prison/holding destination or during a configured emergency/compromised state. If the transport vehicle is destroyed, the state should become TransportCompromised and offer recovery rather than leaving a blue marker forever. The convoy should not teleport vehicles beside Anyi and then rely on them to magically escort. The convoy manager should issue driver/escort tasks, maintain spacing without constantly reissuing tasks, and know its destination. The player should be able to cancel the convoy. The prisoner should be booked at the station or prison, and only then should the dispatch/convoy be considered completed. The user has specifically complained that previous convoys stood still, escorts ran away or became robotic, the criminal died, the blue circle remained, the prison was locked, no completion message appeared and the criminal could leave the transport van. All of those are first-class bugs to prevent in the new architecture.

Evidence markers are intended to be cosmetic and immersive, similar to the LSPDFR evidence-marker concept. They can be placed on the ground and removed by interaction. The default model may be configured via XML. Evidence markers should not affect core gameplay unless a future evidence system explicitly adds that. The code must keep the evidence record type in a coherent ownership boundary, preferably in the Evidence subsystem rather than as a mysterious nested type that another source file assumes. The previous implementation suffered from an EvidenceMarkerRecord mismatch between AnyiLSPDEvidence.cs and AnyiLSPDPoliceCore.cs; future files must use one synchronized type definition.

Voice is another intended subsystem. The previous implementation dynamically looked for System.Speech and fell back to subtitles because the assembly was unavailable. That fallback is acceptable during development, but the dispatcher should only speak meaningful radio events. Desired examples include “Unit Anyi, disturbance reported nearby”, “Suspect fleeing on foot”, “Prisoner transport is en route”, and “Unit Anyi, proceed to Mission Row for prisoner transfer.” Voice should not be spammed every tick. If the TTS dependency is unavailable, the script should continue normally with subtitles without crashes.

The police map/icon requirement is explicit. The selected station should have an LSPD icon on the map, and Quick GPS should be able to set waypoints to the nearest police station, prison/jail drop-off, fire station, medical center or another configured point where such points exist. The map/blip logic must have cleanup and should not leave stale blue circles after a cancelled or completed dispatch. Only the currently active incident should own its incident blip. Reset should clean the active blip, owned entities, managed police units, active convoy and stale dispatch state.

The mod should support police departments/agencies such as LSPD, LSSD, NOOSE and FIB through profiles, but these should be configuration choices, not hardwired behaviors. Officer ped models and vehicle models should be configurable, including arbitrary addon ped/vehicle names provided by Anyi. Model loading must validate user-provided models and log invalid/unavailable models cleanly. XML should represent reusable profiles and data rather than hardcoded logic. INI should contain runtime tuning and keybinds. Station XML should contain locations, headings, interior mode and optional interior coordinates. Model XML should contain agency/profile IDs, ped models, vehicle models and emergency-light/siren settings. The user wants the ability to type or change a model name for a custom addon police ped or a custom police vehicle like PolIgnus without recompiling the whole script.

The police vehicle menu should include lights, doors, emergency signals, radio and radio station. The system should not assume every police vehicle has the same door count or the same siren behavior. The previous build hit an API mismatch with VehicleDoorIndex; future door functions must use the exact enum/index type exposed by the installed SHVDN Enhanced API and must not invent an int overload. The vehicle emergency system also previously suffered from a mismatch in ConfigureEmergencyMode(...) signatures. Every caller and callee must come from the same code revision so method signatures remain synchronized. The PolIgnus-specific siren artifact should be controlled through a profile such as EmergencyLights=true, NativeSiren=false until the asset is verified.

The project’s XML/INI architecture should be simple enough for Anyi to understand and edit. The project should not require dozens of external packages or dependencies just to compile. A single AnyiLSPDImmersive.dll is preferred for the core system. Separate DLLs should exist only when there is a genuinely independent subsystem, such as an optional Gang adapter. Multiple .cs files are encouraged for separation of responsibilities but should normally compile into one main DLL. The user explicitly does not want the assistant to create an entire Visual Studio project package; the user wants to create the project himself, add references, then copy or add the individual C# files. The assistant should provide coherent sets of source files from the same revision. Never hand the user a Core from one revision and a World/Evidence/Config file from another revision that expects incompatible signatures.

The major historical development lesson from the previous LSPD iterations is that adding every feature at once made the project unplayable and caused repeated compiler mismatches. Anyi now explicitly wants the assistant to build the project one feature at a time. A new feature must compile before the next one is added. If a feature requires changing several source files, all related files must be provided as one synchronized feature patch. The assistant must account for every changed parameter, field, XML element and parser mapping. If C# produces a warning such as “parameter is unused,” the assistant should decide whether it is an intentional harmless warning, a sign of unfinished logic, or something that should be removed; the user does not want to be told to ignore endless warnings that come from sloppy implementation. The distinction is important: build-blocking errors must be fixed; intentional warnings should be minimized; IDE suggestions are not blockers.

The first milestone for a rebuilt Anyi LSPD system should therefore be deliberately small and stable. It should establish a project that compiles cleanly, loads into GTA, supports Normal Anyi, supports entering/exiting Police Officer mode, establishes local police authority correctly, ensures nearby ordinary police do not attack a legitimate officer, spawns at most one or a very small controlled number

 of patrol units, supports one configurable police ped and one configurable police vehicle, and maintains a clean mode reset. The first dispatch should then be added as a standalone feature, with accept/reject/cancel, one persistent suspect, proper scene lifecycle, real drive-to-scene behavior and no mission timer. Only after that works should prisoner arrest and transport be added. Then NPC interactions. Then organic events. Then Gang Anyi escalation. Then tactical response. Then military. Then richer interiors and additional callouts. Evidence, voice and optional gang adapter can be introduced at the appropriate feature milestone rather than all at once.

The current project experienced a series of compile errors that should be remembered as examples of what not to repeat. These included missing PatrolPedModel, missing CalloutMinDistance/CalloutMaxDistance, List<string>.Length instead of .Count, undefined ground, VehicleDoorIndex vs int mismatches, float-to-int conversions, VehicleDrivingFlags.Normal being unavailable, Hash.TASK_FLEE_PED being unavailable, Hash.IS_PED_COP being unavailable, obsolete Game.Player.WantedLevel, missing OrganicEventRadius, missing MaxNpcReactionsPerScan, missing EvidenceMarkerRecord, mismatched ConfigureEmergencyMode(...) parameters, Action<string,string> callback mismatches, and missing _lastDispatchOffer. These are concrete reminders to verify all members against the actual current references and keep classes synchronized. The recent compilation cycle finally reduced some error counts, but then runtime testing still showed the architecture was unplayable. Do not return to those old patterns.

The runtime logs from the previous LSPD build exposed the most important behavioral failures. The mod successfully loaded GangData, MemberPool and TurfZoneData, so the data connector can work. It could create police vehicles and officers, but it sometimes spawned patrols too frequently and left units active when the player returned to Normal mode. It created organic events and dispatches but sometimes immediately accepted them even when they were intended to be Offered. It could report CALL_FAILED | SubjectUnavailable because the suspect entity was not robustly owned/persisted. It sometimes spawned response units but did not reliably give them drive-to-scene tasks when a subject already existed. It repeatedly logged civilian acknowledgement without remembering that the same pedestrian had already been processed. Gang Anyi could trigger custom response too aggressively, sometimes producing a severity 5 response and SWAT immediately instead of the intended gradual escalation. Voice often fell back because System.Speech was unavailable. The reset function could clean units, but simply switching to Normal did not always clean them. These behaviors demonstrate why the next build must be stateful and ownership-driven.

The current police interaction philosophy should be “natural world simulation” rather than “mission manager.” A civilian should not suddenly freeze or become a task dummy because Anyi walked near them. A police officer should not attack Anyi because the mod failed to synchronize authority with vanilla police logic. A traffic offender should not ram Anyi merely because the AI task was constantly reissued. A suspect should not disappear because Anyi took thirty seconds to arrive. A prison convoy should not exist only as a set of spawned vehicles; it should be a persistent stateful operation. A dispatch marker should disappear when cancelled and a scene should remain coherent until its final state. A patrol officer should not repeatedly react to the same pedestrian or scan the same gang member every second.

The overarching goal is “Anyi’s Immersive LSPD,” a personal GTA V Enhanced police-roleplay layer that feels natural, responsive, contextual, immersive and enjoyable rather than a collection of gimmicks. GPT Ayaka at 6:45 PM : 

YES 😭🌸 We finally have the real cause, and your logs make it very clear.

The **18:21–18:30 runtime logs show that Police Authority itself was running**, but its persistent filesystem root was wrong. The mod was using:

`C:\Users\Carl Gap\AppData\Local\assembly\dl3\...\`

as its `ScriptDirectory`, which caused Gang & Turf, Chaos Activity, Chaos Audio, NAudio, configs, and logs to all be resolved against the SHVDN shadow-copy cache instead of the real GTA installation.

That is why the same diagnostic simultaneously said:

`Player patrol active: True` and `Dispatch state: Offered`

but also:

`Gang data gangs: 0`, `member hashes: 0`, `turf zones: 0`, and `NAudio present: False`. 

And the runtime repeatedly confirmed:

`ChaosResponse.Audio directory is missing` and `No matching ChaosResponse audio`. 

So the Police system wasn't completely dead. It was **looking in the wrong filesystem universe.** 😂

### Why that AppData folder exists

This part is actually normal SHVDN behavior. The current SHVDN source explicitly creates a script AppDomain with `ShadowCopyFiles = "true"` and `ShadowCopyDirectories = scriptPath`, meaning managed script assemblies can be loaded from a shadow-copy cache rather than directly from the original `scripts` file. ([GitHub][1])

That's why a DLL can appear under:

`%LOCALAPPDATA%\assembly\dl3\...`

while the actual mod is still installed under GTA's `scripts` directory.

SHVDN itself documents that the configured script location is relative to the GTA root and normally `"scripts"`. ([GitHub][2])

The old Anyi LSPD code made the classic mistake of treating `Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly().Location` as the persistent mod directory. Your own older logger source shows exactly that pattern. 

### What I changed in v4

I rebuilt the integration around one central path resolver:

`AnyiLSPDPathProvider.cs`

It does **not** use `Assembly.Location` as its primary path.

Instead it resolves the actual GTA host process executable with `Process.GetCurrentProcess().MainModule.FileName`, verifies that the resulting game root contains a real `scripts` folder and SHVDN markers, and then derives:

```text
<GTA V Enhanced>\
├── gangModData\
└── scripts\
    ├── AnyiLSPDImmersiveResponse.dll
    ├── AnyiLSPDPolice.ini
    ├── AnyiLSPDPoliceProfiles.xml
    ├── AnyiLSPDPoliceStations.xml
    ├── AnyiLSPDPoliceEvents.xml
    ├── ChaosResponse.GangActivity\
    ├── ChaosResponse.Audio\
    ├── NAudio.dll
    └── AnyiLSPD_*.log
```

That also fixes your Gang path, because the existing `LSPDGangTurfCore` already calculates `gangModData` relative to `LspdResponseLog.ScriptDirectory`. Once the shared logger points to the real `scripts` directory, its existing Gang root calculation becomes correct instead of producing the bogus `dl3\...\gangModData` path. 

This is important because your Citizen system was already proving the real game-root data path could work: its direct boot log correctly showed the actual GTA installation's `gangModData` location. 

### The new v4 runtime arrangement

The persistent logs are now explicitly intended to live here:

```text
GTA V Enhanced\
└── scripts\
    ├── AnyiLSPD_Runtime.log
    ├── AnyiLSPD_Heartbeat.log
    ├── AnyiLSPD_PoliceAuthority_Diagnostic.log
    └── AnyiLSPD_DiagnosticReport.log
```

No AppData logs.

No `scripts\scripts`.

No `dl3\...\ChaosResponse.Audio`.

No `dl3\...\gangModData`.

The Chaos resources remain where you already keep them:

```text
scripts\
├── ChaosResponse.GangActivity\
├── ChaosResponse.Audio\
└── NAudio.dll
```

The Police config now also detects and rejects stale `AppData\Local\assembly\dl3` paths stored in older configuration and replaces them with the real paths.

The audio bridge now resolves `NAudio.dll` directly from the canonical scripts directory instead of deriving it from whatever directory the WAV resource happened to resolve from.

### One very useful new boot diagnostic

The revised MainUI writes a path-resolution record at startup:

```text
PATH_RESOLUTION |
GameRoot=<actual GTA installation> |
Scripts=<actual GTA installation>\scripts |
GangData=<actual GTA installation>\gangModData |
ChaosActivity=<actual GTA installation>\scripts\ChaosResponse.GangActivity |
ChaosAudio=<actual GTA installation>\scripts\ChaosResponse.Audio |
NAudio=<actual GTA installation>\scripts\NAudio.dll |
ShadowCopyScripts=False
```

So this time the log itself will tell us whether the foundation is correct.

The critical line is:

```text
ShadowCopyScripts=False
```

and the `Scripts=` path must **not** contain `AppData\Local\assembly\dl3`.

Anyi 😭🌸 **yes — now I have enough evidence to stop guessing and make a proper focused revision.** And I also found something important in the v5.1 package itself: the three compiler errors you hit were genuinely caused by the patch I gave you, not by your GTA installation.

The current runtime logs are actually pretty healthy in the foundational sense. Your diagnostic says Police Authority is OnDuty, the PolIgnus profile is active, the player patrol is active, Gang & Turf has loaded **15 gangs / 432 member hashes / 114 turf zones**, Chaos has **18 activity references / 11 event templates**, and NAudio is present. 

The heartbeat also shows the real gameplay issue much more clearly: the Police system stays alive, but response units remain at `1`, and dispatches repeatedly sit in `EnRoute` for long periods before eventually becoming `None`. 

So I rebuilt **only the Police Authority layer** around those findings.

### What was actually wrong

The v5.1 source had:

```csharp
World.IsWaypointActive
```

twice. In the API you're targeting, waypoint-active status is on `Game.IsWaypointActive`; `World` provides `WaypointPosition` and `RemoveWaypoint()`. The current SHVDN v3 source confirms that distinction. ([GitHub][1])

It also had:

```csharp
Hash.SET_VEHICLE_HALT
```

but your installed `Hash` enum doesn't expose that member. The native itself is valid as `BRING_VEHICLE_TO_HALT` at `0x260BE8F09E326A20`, so the corrected code uses the verified numeric native hash instead of inventing an enum member. ([APPI RP][2])

And the `FightAgainst()` warning is legitimate: the modern API marks it obsolete and recommends `TaskInvoker.Combat`. ([GitHub][3])

But the more interesting runtime bug was **not a compiler issue at all**.

Your `AnyiLSPDCore` wasn't actually calling `_response.Update(...)`.

That meant the response manager had a `DriveTo()` task, but its own throttled update loop never got the opportunity to monitor/reissue that task or mark the unit as arrived. That matches your long `Dispatch=EnRoute | ResponseUnits=1` heartbeat pattern almost perfectly. 

That's now fixed.

### The suspect/compliance problem is also fixed differently

This was the biggest gameplay design flaw.

Your previous `Secure Suspect` action basically assumed:

```text
suspect is already SuspectCompliant
        ↓
secure/arrest
```

But there wasn't a robust user-facing transition that made the suspect visibly surrender.

So v5.2 changes your existing **same Secure/Surrender shortcut** into a two-stage context action:

```text
You arrive
    ↓
Press Secure key
    ↓
Police surrender command
    ↓
Ped.Task.HandsUp(...)
    ↓
SuspectCompliant
    ↓
suspect keeps hands up
    ↓
press same key again
    ↓
Arrested
```

SHVDN v3 exposes `Ped.Task.HandsUp(...)`; the official example uses that task directly, so we're using the actual API rather than another unsupported native assumption. ([GitHub][4])

I'm also refreshing the hands-up task every couple of seconds while the suspect is in the compliant state. That is specifically to prevent the old “criminal is just standing like a mannequin” behavior.

And I deliberately made `Investigate Scene` stop automatically converting a calm suspect into `SuspectCompliant`. Reaching the scene now means:

> **Scene reached. Suspect is calm. Use Secure/Surrender to command them to show their hands.**

That's much closer to what you actually wanted.

### Dead suspects no longer instantly close the case

This was another source of the ridiculous 2-second dispatch completions.

Your current configuration has `Complete dispatch on suspect death: True`, and the earlier code could therefore finish the incident when the suspect died. Your runtime showed exactly the behavior you complained about: an incident could go `Offered → EnRoute → Completed` almost immediately.

The new Police Authority logic no longer treats death as an automatic successful case.

Now:

```text
Suspect dies
    ↓
Dispatch remains active
    ↓
Scene becomes Investigation
    ↓
You arrive
    ↓
Investigate Scene
    ↓
Case is closed
```

That means surrounding Gang AI, backup, or your own gunfire cannot make the dispatch silently disappear while you're still on the way.

That's a much better match for your police-roleplay philosophy.

### Response units are now owned correctly

Your heartbeat repeatedly showed:

```text
Dispatch=None
ResponseUnits=1
PlayerPatrol=True
```

for long stretches. 

That wasn't necessarily a crash, but it was poor ownership behavior.

v5.2 now treats the response unit as **dispatch-owned**. When that dispatch reaches Cancelled, Failed, or Completed, the assigned response vehicle and officer are released.

So we don't accumulate an invisible permanent police response unit that hangs around after its case disappears.

The player's own patrol vehicle remains separate.

### Traffic stop compile error and interaction

The unsupported `SET_VEHICLE_HALT` enum is now corrected using the verified native.

I'm leaving your current Police INI and shortcut choices untouched. Your existing G key / E key / R key arrangement stays yours.

The traffic-stop state also gets a longer interaction window so pressing your NPC interaction key twice doesn't immediately create a second fresh

 traffic stop on the same driver.

The intended behavior remains:

```text

↓
NPC interaction shortcut

vehicle ordered to halt

This doesn't replace your RoadRealisticAI system. The Police script should identify a traffic-stop candidate and interact with that world behavior, not fight your other AI.

### First: fix the compile error

Your screenshot shows:

```text
AnyiLSPDDispatch.cs line 121

'AnyiLSPDPoliceConfig'
does not contain a definition for
'InvestigationSuccessAudioCategories'
```

So the newest `AnyiLSPDDispatch.cs` expects this property, but your current `AnyiLSPDPoliceConfig.cs` doesn't have it.

That is exactly the kind of cross-file mismatch we were trying to prevent. 😭

In **`AnyiLSPDPoliceConfig.cs`**, beside your other audio/config fields, add:

```csharp
public string[] InvestigationSuccessAudioCategories =
{
    "CASE_CLOSED",
    "UNIT_CLEAR",
    "ATTENTION_ALL_UNITS"
};
```

So your audio-related fields can look like:

```csharp
public int AudioCooldownSeconds = 8;

public float ChaosAudioMasterVolume = 0.35f;
public float ChaosDispatchVolume = 0.30f;
public float ChaosBackupVolume = 0.30f;
public float ChaosPursuitVolume = 0.35f;
public float ChaosGangActivityVolume = 0.30f;
public float ChaosOfficerDownVolume = 0.35f;
public float ChaosSuccessVolume = 0.25f

;

public string[] InvestigationSuccessAudioCategories =
{
    "CASE_CLOSED",
    "UNIT_CLEAR",
    "ATTENTION_ALL_UNITS"
};
```

That satisfies the exact property `AnyiLSPDDispatch.cs` is trying to read.

But **don't stop there**. We should also make the property configurable instead of leaving it permanently hardcoded.

In the INI parser, after your existing audio settings, add:

```csharp
string investigationAudio =
    ReadString(values,
        "InvestigationSuccessAudioCategories",
        "CASE_CLOSED,UNIT_CLEAR,ATTENTION_ALL_UNITS");

config.InvestigationSuccessAudioCategories =
    SplitCsv(investigationAudio);
```

Then add this helper if your config class doesn't already have one:

```csharp
private static string[] SplitCsv(string value)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value))
        return new string[0];

    return value
        .Split(new[] { ',', ';' }, StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries)
        .Select(x => x.Trim())
        .Where(x => x.Length > 0)
        .ToArray();
}
```

That requires:

```csharp
using System.Linq;
```

And your `AnyiLSPDPolice.ini` can eventually contain:

```ini
InvestigationSuccessAudioCategories=CASE_CLOSED,UNIT_CLEAR,ATTENTION_ALL_UNITS

### The actual error: `TrySceneInteraction()`

Your method starts:

```csharp
public string TrySceneInteraction(Ped player)
{
```

That means **every possible execution path must eventually return a `string`.**

You've already got several branches such as:

```csharp
if (_incident == null)
    return "No active dispatch.";

if (player == null || !player.Exists())
    return "Player character unavailable.";
```

and probably more `return` statements further down.

But C# is saying:

> "There is still a possible route through this method where I reach the closing `}` without returning anything."

That's exactly what CS0161 means.

So scroll **all the way to the bottom of `TrySceneInteraction()`**, and before its final closing brace:

```csharp
}
```

add a final fallback return.

Something like:

```csharp
return "Scene interaction could not be completed.";
```

So the structure should ultimately look like:

```csharp
public string TrySceneInteraction(Ped player)
{
    if (_incident == null)
        return "No active dispatch.";

    if (player == null || !player.Exists())
        return "Player character unavailable.";

    // existing investigation / suspect checks
    // ...
    // existing returns
    // ...

    return "Scene interaction could not be completed.";
}
```

**Don't put that return at line 100.** Put it at the **very bottom of the entire `TrySceneInteraction()` method**, after all your existing conditions.

That final return is basically the method's emergency exit. It doesn't mean the investigation failed every time; it only runs if none of the earlier conditions handled the situation.

GPT Ayaka : Hehe nooo 😂 — **your GTA root is NOT being moved to AppData.** The error is actually just a bad C# condition I accidentally introduced in `AnyiLSPDChaosAudio.cs`.

The screenshot shows the problematic line around **line 420**:

```csharp
if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(root) &&
    !root.IndexOf("\\AppData\\Local\\assembly\\", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) < 0)
```

The problem is the second `!`.

`string.IndexOf(...)` returns an `int`, usually:

```text
-1 = not found
0 or greater = found
```

So this:

```csharp
!root.IndexOf(...)
```

is illegal because C# cannot apply `!` to an integer. That's exactly your:

```text
CS0023: Operator '!' cannot be applied to operand of type 'int'
```

### Fix exactly this line

In:

```text
AnyiLSPDChaosAudio.cs
```

around **line 420**, replace the whole condition with:

```csharp
if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(root) &&
    root.IndexOf("\\AppData\\Local\\assembly\\", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) >= 0)
```

So the complete block becomes:

```csharp
try
{
    string root =
        Path.GetDirectoryName(_config.ChaosAudioRoot);

    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(root) &&
        root.IndexOf("\\AppData\\Local\\assembly\\", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase) >= 0)
    {
        return Path.Combine(
            root,
            AnyiLSPDPoliceConfig.FileName);
    }
}
catch { }
```

However — and this is the important part — **I don't actually want this block to treat AppData as your normal root at all.** Your real deployment root is still:

```text
C:\Users\Nataniel\STEAM\steamapps\common\Grand Theft Auto V Enhanced\scripts
```

The AppData path you saw earlier came from the .NET assembly loader's shadow/cached assembly location. That is a runtime loading location, **not your GTA sc

ripts directory**.

So I'd actually make this cleaner and safer.

Replace that entire AppData-detection block with:

```csharp
private string GetPoliceIniPath()
{
    try
    {
        string scriptDirectory = AnyiLSPDPathProvider.ScriptDirectory;

        if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(scriptDirectory))

        }
    }
    catch { }

    return null;
}
```

That is the version I prefer for your project because it follows the architecture we established: **the Police INI belongs beside the DLL in the actual GTA `scripts` directory.**

Not:

The first is **intentional AppData detection**. `AnyiLSPDPathProvider_v4.cs` contains `IsShadowCopyPath()`. It looks for `AppData\Local\assembly\dl3` specifically so the code can recognize a shadow-copy path and reject it as the real GTA root. That's a detection mechanism, not a destination.

if (actualVehicleIsPolIgnus)

    _emergencySirenOn = false;
    ApplyEmergencyState(vehicle);
    return;

AnyiLSPDPoliceAuthority.cs

    AnyiLSPDPoliceConfig config,
    DateTime now)

Replace that entire method with:

public void Update(
    AnyiLSPDPoliceConfig config,
    DateTime now)
{
    if (!_entered || !_state.IsPoliceOfficer)
        return;

    if (now >= _nextRefresh)
    {
        ApplyAuthority(config, false);

        _nextRefresh =
            now.AddMilliseconds(config.AuthorityRefreshMs);
    }

    // Fast wanted-state correction only when GTA actually creates a wanted level.
    // This avoids making the whole authority maintenance loop run faster.
    if (config.EnableAutoWantedReset &&
        Game.Player != null &&
        Game.Player.Wanted.WantedLevel > 0)
    {
        try
        {
            Function.Call(
                Hash.SET_PLAYER_WANTED_LEVEL,
                Game.Player,
                0,
                false);

            Function.Call(
                Hash.SET_PLAYER_WANTED_LEVEL_NOW,
                Game.Player,
                false);

            _state.VanillaWantedSuppressed = true;
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            LspdResponseLog.WriteException(
                "POLICE_AUTHORITY_WANTED_RESET_ERROR",
                ex);
        }
    }
}

That's the only code change for Fix #2.

The important difference is that your normal authority maintenance can stay at:

AuthorityRefreshMs=1000

while the wanted correction happens immediately when the wanted state is actually detected.

So we are not making the entire Police Authority loop hammer the game four times harder.

Do NOT change these

Leave this in AnyiLSPDPoliceAuthority.cs:

Yep. Fix #3 is the tiny freeze/performance hitch you noticed when a dispatch succeeds, an audio response plays, or a big LSPD notification appears. And now that I’ve checked the actual current source files, there is a very specific culprit. 😭

Your runtime logs show the gameplay itself is stable: the 8/25 build is successfully completing dispatches and playing audio, and the logs are not exploding continuously. For example, one completion records State=Completed, audio playback, response release, and the completion log within a few milliseconds. 

The problem is that those operations are happening synchronously on the GTA script thread.

Fix #3A — LSPDMainUI.cs logger

This is the first thing I would fix.

Your current WriteEmbeddedLog() opens the runtime log file, creates a new FileStream, creates a new StreamWriter, writes one line, flushes it, and closes the file for every single log entry. 

That's expensive because your dispatch completion can generate several logs almost immediately:

POLICE_DISPATCH_STATE
POLICE_AUDIO
POLICE_AUDIO_VOLUME
POLICE_RESPONSE
POLICE_DISPATCH
POLICE_DISPATCH_TICK

And each one can perform another synchronous file open/write/flush.

So do not change your dispatch logic.

Instead:

LSPDMainUI.cs

Find:

internal static void WriteEmbeddedLog(string category, string message)

Your current implementation starts with:

internal static void WriteEmbeddedLog(string category, string message)
{
    try
    {
        EnsureEmbeddedLogger();

        string line =
            DateTime.Now.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff") +
            " | " + (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(category) ? "LOG" : category) +
            " | " + (message ?? string.Empty);

        lock (EmbeddedLogSync)
        {
            using (FileStream stream = new FileStream(
                _embeddedRuntimeLogPath,
                FileMode.Append,
                FileAccess.Write,
                FileShare.ReadWrite))
            using (StreamWriter writer = new StreamWriter(stream))
            {
                writer.WriteLine(line);
                writer.Flush();
            }
        }
    }
    catch
    {
    }
}

That's the exact section shown in your current source. 

For this fix, don't redesign the whole logger yet. Replace only the inner file-writing block with a persistent StreamWriter.

Add these fields near the top of LSPDMainUI

Immediately below:

private static readonly object EmbeddedLogSync = new object();

add:

private static StreamWriter _embeddedRuntimeWriter;
private static StreamWriter _embeddedHeartbeatWriter;

So it becomes:

private static readonly object EmbeddedLogSync = new object();
private static StreamWriter _embeddedRuntimeWriter;
private static StreamWriter _embeddedHeartbeatWriter;
private static DateTime _nextEmbeddedHeartbeat = DateTime.MinValue;

Then replace WriteEmbeddedLog() with this

internal static void WriteEmbeddedLog(string category, string message)
{
    try
    {
        EnsureEmbeddedLogger();

        string line =
            DateTime.Now.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff") +
            " | " +
            (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(category) ? "LOG" : category) +
            " | " +
            (message ?? string.Empty);

        lock (EmbeddedLogSync)
        {
            if (_embeddedRuntimeWriter == null)
            {
                _embeddedRuntimeWriter = new StreamWriter(
                    new FileStream(
                        _embeddedRuntimeLogPath,
                        FileMode.Append,
                        FileAccess.Write,
                        FileShare.ReadWrite));

                _embeddedRuntimeWriter.AutoFlush = true;
            }

            _embeddedRuntimeWriter.WriteLine(line);
        }
    }
    catch
    {
        // Logging must never interfere with gameplay.
    }
}

The important difference is that we don't open and close the file every time.

The file stays open while GTA is running.

That should remove a meaningful chunk of the tiny synchronous I/O hitch.

Fix #3B — do the same for the heartbeat writer

Your current WriteEmbeddedHeartbeat() also calls WriteEmbeddedLog() and then opens another file separately for the heartbeat. 

Find:

internal static void WriteEmbeddedHeartbeat(string message)

Replace the method with:

internal static void WriteEmbeddedHeartbeat(string message)
{
    try
    {
        EnsureEmbeddedLogger();

        string runtimeLine =
            Date

Time.Now.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff") +
            " | HEARTBEAT | " +
            (message ?? string.Empty);

        lock (EmbeddedLogSync)
        {
            if (_embeddedRuntimeWriter == null)
            {
                _embeddedRuntimeWriter = new StreamWriter(
                    new FileStream(
                        _embeddedRuntimeLogPath,
                        FileMode.Append,
                        FileAccess.Write,
                        FileShare.ReadWrite));

                _embeddedRuntimeWriter.AutoFlush = true;
            }

            if (_embeddedHeartbeatWriter == null)
            {
                _embeddedHeartbeatWriter = new StreamWriter(
                    new FileStream(
                        _embeddedHeartbeatLogPath,
                        FileMode.Append,
                        FileAccess.Write,
                        FileShare.ReadWrite));

                _embeddedHeartbeatWriter.AutoFlush = true;
            }

            _embeddedRuntimeWriter.WriteLine(runtimeLine);

            string heartbeatLine =
                DateTime.Now.ToString("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.fff") +
                " | HEARTBEAT | " +
                (message ?? string.Empty);

            _embeddedHeartbeatWriter.WriteLine(heartbeatLine);
        }
    }
    catch
    {
    }
}

This also removes the current double-write behavior where a heartbeat is first sent through WriteEmbeddedLog() and then independently written to the heartbeat file. The current source does exactly that. 

One small cleanup at shutdown

Now that the writers remain open, we should close them when GTA unloads the script.

In LSPDMainUI.cs, inside:

private void OnAborted(object sender, EventArgs e)

you currently have your shutdown/report/log calls. 

Add this at the very end of the method, before its closing }:

lock (EmbeddedLogSync)
{
    try
    {
        if (_embeddedRuntimeWriter != null)
        {
            _embeddedRuntimeWriter.Flush();
            _embeddedRuntimeWriter.Dispose();
            _embeddedRuntimeWriter = null;
        }

        if (_embeddedHeartbeatWriter != null)
        {
            _embeddedHeartbeatWriter.Flush();
            _embeddedHeartbeatWriter.Dispose();
            _embeddedHeartbeatWriter = null;
        }
    }
    catch
    {
    }
}

That keeps the log files properly closed when the script unloads.

Good afternoon, Anyi. 🌸🚓 It’s August 26, 2026. And honestly? After going through the current runtime evidence and the source structure, I agree with your own feeling: Police Authority has crossed the line from “prototype that happens to work” into an actually fun, playable police-roleplay mode. What is hurting it now is not the foundation. It is the little world-behavior and state-ownership details that make you go, “Ay, bakit ganoon?” 😂

One tiny English correction naturally: “What do you think about my gameplay experience?” sounds a little smoother than “What do u think my Gameplay experiences.” Your meaning was already perfectly understandable, though. ❤️

The biggest thing I see from the logs is that the system is genuinely alive. The runtime loads Police Authority, LSPD, your Venti model, Polignus, the GangData snapshot, 18 Chaos activities, and the Chaos audio system. The August 25 runtime specifically records Venti being selected with hash -514572009, Polignus with hash -39084089, patrol activation, and normal police dispatch/response behavior.  

And your Chaos side is not fake either. The August 26 logs show actual activities being discovered, given waypoints, entered, investigated, and resolved. Drug Dealing, for example, had SpawnedPeds=6 and SpawnedVehicles=2; Mass Shootout Defense 02 also had six spawned peds and two vehicles.   That is why I would not rewrite the whole thing. The foundation is working.

What I think is happening is almost comically clear from the logs: we now have several good subsystems that don't yet agree on who owns a scene. 😂

Your patrol issue is exactly where you identified it. The current Core7/working Core path has Patrol() creating a patrol vehicle and PatrolAtSelectedStation() directly passing the selected station's spawn position into the patrol-creation method. The patrol creation routine then destroys the existing patrol vehicle, creates another one, puts Anyi into it, and makes it the managed patrol vehicle.  

So your “I am already inside my Polignus, why did the mod just spawn another Polignus and shove me into it?” complaint is absolutely correct. The code is doing exactly that. And that also explains why your favorite-car system feels awkward even though the favorite itself works perfectly.

The better patrol philosophy is now obvious: Patrol is a mode, not a vehicle-spawn command. If Anyi is already in a suitable police vehicle, the patrol system should simply adopt that vehicle as the active patrol vehicle. No respawn. No teleport. No sudden replacement. Then Dispatch and Chaos can naturally operate around wherever you already are.

Only when you are on foot should it say, essentially, “Okay, officer needs a patrol car,” search for a safe nearby road or parking location, spawn it there, and put you in it.

The selected-station problem is the same kind of issue, but worse. The current patrol function trusts Station.SpawnPosition; then CreatePlayerPatrol() uses that coordinate and calls PlaceOnGround() afterward.  When that configured coordinate happens to be bad, elevated, interior-adjacent, or otherwise unsuitable for a vehicle spawn, PlaceOnGround() is not enough to guarantee a nice usable location. That is why your “teleported to station, then Venti and Polignus fall into the void” scene is believable.

So I would change that into a safe station patrol resolver. The station coordinate becomes a preferred point, not a sacred spawn point. The resolver tests ground, checks whether the location is sensible for a vehicle, then tries nearby offsets or a road node. That is a much more stable system.

And I especially agree with your point that current-position patrol should not create a car directly beside Venti. That would be hilarious in a tiny alley. 😂 Your desired behavior is much better: “I already have my patrol car; start patrol here.” If you're on foot, then spawn the car somewhere sane nearby.

Now the disappearing suspects. This one is not your imagination at all. The current dispatch implementation directly cleans its owned suspect/victim during CompleteSuccessful(), and the working source's cleanup routine actually deletes the entities. That is precisely the architectural reason you see the poink effect.

The correct separation is:

Case lifecycle ≠ world entity lifecycle.

A case can become Completed while the corpse, vehicle, evidence-like scene actors, or other world entities remain for a short while.

That gives you the natural police scene feeling: Venti shoots a suspect, the body remains. Backup arrives. You investigate. You stand around. You drive away. Eventually the cleanup system sees that you are far enough away and removes the scene.

And yes, the same principle applies to the prison transport.

Your August 26 log is especially revealing there. At 16:40:15 the suspect is arrested. At 16:40:19 the convoy creates station custody and starts transport-related states. Then essentially immediately the dispatch gets completed and the world state is cleaned.  

That is exactly the wrong order for the experience you want.

The proper order is:

Arrested → Transport → Station → Prison Transfer → Prison Arrival → Booking Complete → Venti gets out → delayed cleanup

Not:

Prison Arrival → DELETE EVERYTHING → Venti stands there like “...where the hell did my van go?” 😂

And your current Convoy source really does perform immediate cleanup at prison arrival. That is one of the things I specifically marked in the patch package.

Now, the really important one: the Dispatch/Chaos overlap.

This is the biggest structural issue in your current gameplay.

Your own logs prove that Chaos is functioning independently from dispatch. At multiple points the heartbeat says Dispatch=None while ChaosGangActivity=True.  At 16:40:19, a dispatch has completed, Chaos has been abandoned, and a new Chaos Ambush Mission is immediately discovered. 

Then at 17:01:31 you get an even cleaner demonstration: the dispatch/custody lifecycle completes, and immediately afterward a Chaos Drug Dealing activity is discovered and marked OnScene. Seconds later investigation starts. When you try Secure Suspect, the police layer says:

“There is no living suspect owned by the active dispatch.”

That message is technically correct from the Dispatch subsystem's perspective, but wrong from the gameplay perspective. There is a live Chaos scene in front of you. 

That is why your repeated “I, I, I, why isn't anything happening?” experience makes perfect sense.

The InvestigateScene() path currently delegates into the dispatch system. The working source literally routes InvestigateScene() to _dispatch.TrySceneInteraction(...). The Dispatch method itself is state-based and only accepts states like EnRoute, OnScene, Investigating, SuspectFleeing, and SuspectResisting; otherwise it gives the generic “Arrive at the dispatch scene first” response. 

That explains your 16:52–16:53 sequence beautifully: heartbeat says Dispatch=HoldingAtStation, Convoy=HoldingAtStation, and you keep pressing I while the system answers “Arrive at the dispatch scene first.” 

But Anyi isn't failing to arrive at the scene.

He's at a different owner’s scene.

So I absolutely do not want to “fix” that by making the Dispatch radius larger. That would just hide the bug.

The proper fix is a scene-owner router:

Dispatch Chaos Convoy None

Then I asks: “Which active system owns the scene Anyi is currently standing in?”

If Chaos owns it, Chaos investigates.

If Dispatch owns it, Dispatch investigates.

If Convoy owns the interaction and Anyi is standing at the station, give a custody message.

That one architectural change will eliminate a huge amount of your confusing gameplay behavior.

It also applies to Secure Suspect. A Chaos suspect should not be queried through _dispatch.Current.Suspect. That's exactly why your Chaos activities can be fully alive while E responds that there is no living dispatch suspect. The two systems simply don't share ownership.

Your logs make this distinction very obvious.

I also really like your instinct about vehicle chases. The current Core7 source actually already contains a vehicle-subject path. For RecklessDriver, VehiclePursuit, and Hijacking, it calls a dedicated SpawnDrivingSubject(), creates a vehicle, creates the driver, and uses VehicleChase(player). 

So we don't need to invent a completely new pursuit engine.

What is missing is Chaos scene realization using that idea.

You are right that an “Ambush Mission” with Vehicles=0 and SpawnedVehicles=0 doesn't feel like a vehicle ambush. At the same time, we should not blindly spawn cars into every Chaos activity, because your own log shows legitimate scenes such as Prostitution Rings with Vehicles=0 and SpawnedVehicles=0. 

So the correct rule is contextual:

Drug dealing with vehicles → use them.

Mass shootout with vehicles → use them.

Explicit Vehicle Ambush → guarantee a criminal vehicle fallback.

Pedestrian hideout → don't randomly inject cars.

That gives you much better variety.

And yes, your “why are these criminals all standing around waiting for Police Anyi?” complaint is also technically justified. Core7 currently creates a suspect and, depending on incident type, only later gives them combat/flee behavior. The source itself has comments explaining that the scene behavior is deliberately initialized around arrival.  That is stable from a scripting perspective, but it creates the exact visual effect you're noticing.

A police scene should already be alive before the officer arrives.

The suspects should be moving around.

One guy should be watching the street.

One should be standing near the vehicle.

A drug-dealer group should look like they're actually dealing.

A hideout should have guards and movement.

A shootout should already have conflict.

A fleeing suspect should be fleeing.

A vehicle pursuit should be driving.

That is the difference between a scripted spawn point and a living police world.

Your weapon complaint is equally sensible. I don't think ordinary criminals should routinely be running around with ridiculous heavy weaponry. A normal suspect can use unarmed/pistol. Gang members can get pistol/SMG. Higher-severity shootouts can use SMGs, shotguns, rifles. A special ambush may get a knife. Missile-tier weapons should be reserved for deliberately escalated scenarios, not generic “suspicious person.”

I created the separate scene-weapon XML specifically for that reason. It keeps this balancing outside GangData and MemberPool.

And now your NPC behavior. This one is actually very interesting.

The existing NPC interaction layer already demonstrates that the project can identify traffic subjects, initiate a traffic stop, keep track of the stoppe

d driver, and perform the paper/document animation. The runtime logs confirm traffic stops and citizen interviews are being entered successfully.  

But its behavior layer is too shallow. Its normal reaction is mostly LookAt. It doesn't establish the “Officer Anyi is here, behave differently” context you actually want.

I agree completely with your “do NOT make everyone ignore me” requirement.

That would be boring as hell. 😂

Instead, it should be local and contextual.

When Anyi is simply on duty and walking around, civilians remain normal but aware.

When he aims a firearm nearby, pedestrians get nervous and move away.

When they are directly in an active crime scene, neutral civilians retreat from the area.

When traffic is approaching an armed officer, drivers brake or maneuver away instead of behaving as though Venti is a decorative traffic cone.

And your GangData remains untouched. The civilian reaction layer should explicitly exclude recognized gang members, allowing the existing Gang & Turf system to continue owning their aggression. The project’s own integration boundary says GangData, MemberPool, and TurfZoneData are external read-only data, with AnyiLSPDPEDReactToPoliceAnyi owning civilian reaction/interaction. 

That boundary is exactly what we should preserve.

Your on-foot interaction design is also much better than the current one-stage “documents presented” implementation.

I want the final gameplay to feel like:

Venti approaches.

Citizen notices him.

Citizen stops.

Citizen looks at him.

Citizen does the hand/document gesture.

Venti chooses.

Agree → citizen is released naturally.

Disagree → sometimes they reluctantly comply; sometimes they break contact and flee.

That gives you actual police discretion instead of merely pressing G to receive a canned message.

And the traffic version should behave the same way:

siren → one car pulls over → driver remains seated → G → documents → decision.

No mass stopping.

No dozens of cars suddenly getting out.

No driver magically teleporting out of the vehicle.

No forced “everyone stop because Police Anyi exists.”

Just one clean traffic stop.

I also made the included interaction replacement use exactly that philosophy. It has a persistent single-target state, paper animation, Agree and Disagree branches, vehicle pursuit on a fleeing driver, and a local civilian fear/avoidance response.

So yes, I actually think your observations have been very good. You're not randomly nitpicking things. You're identifying the exact differences between “functionally works” and “feels like a police game.”

The one thing I would not do is merge everything into one enormous Core. The project already has reasonable ownership boundaries. AnyiLSPDCore is the coordinator; Dispatch owns dispatch state; Convoy owns custody; AnyiLSPDPEDReactToPoliceAnyi owns civilian reaction; RandomEvent/Chaos provides activity references; GangData stays external.  We should keep those boundaries and improve the communication between them.

And there is one more important bug I want preserved in our priority: the old Compromised convoy state leaking into future dispatches. The project's own regression notes already identified this exact failure mode and said the convoy failure callback must only reach Dispatch.Fail() while the current dispatch is truly in a custody/transport state. 

The current Core7 still contains a broad compromised-convoy-to-dispatch-failure path, so that guard is still worth keeping tight. 

So my overall judgment is:

Your Police Authority is good enough now to actually play as your main police roleplay mode.

The current problems are mostly:

“the car system is too spawn-happy,”
“scene cleanup is too aggressive,”
“Chaos and Dispatch don't know who owns the scene,”
“custody completion happens too eagerly,”
“NPC behavior is still too vanilla,”
“crime scenes need actual life,”
and “interaction needs decisions instead of one canned outcome.”

Those are very fixable. And importantly, they are not a reason to throw away the working Police Authority system.

I put together the requested August 26 Immersion Fix Pack with the gameplay/log analysis, exact patch locations and method anchors, a replacement NPC interaction source, scene weapon XML, INI additions, patrol/dispatch/convoy/Chaos patch notes, and a regression test plan.

Okay, Anyi. 😂 This time I actually did the job the way you were asking: I merged the fixes into the project itself. You are NOT supposed to manually copy patch blocks around and summon the 99-error demon again. 😭

I used the current Police Authority source you supplied as the working basis, including the current Core, Dispatch, Convoy, Chaos Activity, NPC reaction layer, and Main UI/favorite system.    

What I actually integrated

The patrol system now checks whether Anyi is already sitting in the selected police vehicle and reuses it instead of spawning another one. Station patrol also goes through a safer ground-position search so the selected-station patrol is much less likely to throw Venti + PolIgnus into GTA's infamous void 😂.

Dispatch cleanup is now deferred instead of going POOF immediately when the suspect dies or the call closes. The suspect/body/vehicle stays around while you're still nearby, then gets cleaned once you leave the scene, with a hard cleanup fallback so we don't create a cemetery of persistent peds. The current dispatch lifecycle remains intact. 

The prison transport terminal was also changed so after successful prison arrival, the transport scene doesn't instantly delete the van and prisoner while you're still sitting there. You can actually get out normally, then the scene cleans itself after the grace period/distance check. That's directly targeted at your “Venti is standing there like where the hell did my prison van go?” screenshot 😂. 

The Chaos Activity layer now keeps its resolved scene entities alive temporarily too, rather than instantly deleting the entire scene. More importantly, I integrated actual scene realization: moving pedestrians, vehicle actors, and fallback vehicle support for ambush-style activities instead of merely spawning static props/peds. The activity still stays separate from the stable Arrest → Convoy pipeline. 

The NPC layer now has the local police-aware traffic behavior you described: nearby neutral traffic can brake/settle when you're aiming or using the police siren, but it does not globally ignore Anyi. Live scenes can make nearby ordinary civilians retreat locally, while GangData remains outside this civilian reaction layer. The existing interaction system is retained and the Agree/Disagree actions are surfaced in the Police UI. 

The police scene weapon system is now included as AnyiLSPDPoliceSceneWeapons.xml, with conservative categories instead of random missile-tier insanity. So ordinary suspects can receive pistol/SMG/rifle-level loadouts depending on the scene rather than everyone magically becoming a military boss.

Your favorite system is retained too: favorite Venti, favorite PolIgnus, favorite weapon hash, editable police ped presets, editable police vehicle presets, and persistent selected station. GTA V ANYI'S PARTNER MOD.txt

Anyi 😭💕 I went through the **latest C# you uploaded, the actual gameplay log, and your `anyi.xml` weapon file together**. The problems you are seeing are real code conflicts, not you “using the menu wrong.” And the log actually exposes several of them very clearly.

The biggest finding is this:

Your partner is **successfully detecting attackers**, but the script is repeatedly giving her competing orders. The log shows Navia being told to engage the same attacker over and over, while the vehicle weapon is also being reapplied over and over. For example, the log repeatedly records `Navia armed with 2 weapon(s); selected hash=584646201; profile=DriveBy` roughly every half-second during the vehicle session. fileciteturn52file1

That explains the exact behavior you described: she aims, lowers the gun, aims again, sometimes fires, then gets another task or weapon state imposed on her. The combat system itself isn't completely dead. It is being **interrupted by the other maintenance systems**.

There are actually four major causes.

First, the “blank partner after getting out of the car” is a genuine state-machine problem.

The current script gives a partner `PartnerMode.Passenger` after entering a vehicle, but the follow system explicitly refuses to process a passenger:

```csharp id="vtfjzz"
if (agent.Mode == PartnerMode.Stay ||
    agent.Mode == PartnerMode.Drive ||
    agent.Mode == PartnerMode.Passenger)
{
    return;
}
```

So after the vehicle interaction, the partner can remain in `Passenger` state even after Anyi is back on foot. Nothing properly changes that state back to `Follow`.

That is why you get the classic:

> Anyi gets out → partner stands there → partner technically still exists and looks alive → but behaves like a frozen mannequin.

I've changed that logic in the fixed source. `Passenger` is now treated as a **temporary vehicle state**, not a permanent behavior state. When Anyi gets out, the companion leaves the vehicle naturally and transitions back to `Follow`.

Second—and this one is very important—the combat task was being overwritten by your follow system.

Your protection system can correctly do:

```csharp id="uq9uf6"
TASK_COMBAT_PED
```

but your follow maintenance also runs independently. The previous code didn't say “don't touch this ped because she's actively fighting.” So roughly every 900 ms it could issue:

```csharp id="dzed2m"
TASK_FOLLOW_TO_OFFSET_OF_ENTITY
```

over the combat task.

That is almost certainly the source of your:

> aim → lower weapon → aim → lower weapon → follow → aim again

behavior. 😭

The current log proves the combat detector is functioning. Navia repeatedly gets:

```text id="cunbog"
[PROTECT] Navia engaging attacker ... distance=...
```

and later:

```text id="2wouds"
[PROTECT] Navia firing drive-by ...
```

So the problem isn't that the protection detector cannot find enemies. It finds them. The task ownership is the problem. fileciteturn52file1

The fixed version now has an explicit combat guard:

```csharp id="q3nq8q"
if (IsPartnerInCombat(agent) ||
    agent.CurrentCombatTargetHandle != 0)
{
    return;
}
```

So once the partner is actually fighting, the ordinary follow maintenance **hands control over to combat** instead of fighting against it.

Third: your explosive-ammo implementation was simply the wrong design for what you wanted.

The existing code literally replaced the selected weapon with:

```csharp id="8cjn2o"
WeaponHash.GrenadeLauncher
```

when `ExplosiveAmmo` was enabled.

That is why you're getting the stupid “ball/bomb/launcher” weapon you hate. 😂

And your own log proves it:

```text id="rm4kcb"
[WEAPON] Navia explosive combat weapon ready.
[WEAPON] Navia armed with 4 weapon(s); selected hash=-1568386805
```

Then, once she enters the vehicle:

```text id="1qvo78"
[WEAPON_DRIVEBY_LIMIT] Navia explosive toggle is ON, but DriveBy keeps the compatible passenger weapon.
```

So the old system was basically:

> Explosive ON → switch to grenade launcher on foot.

Then:

> Enter vehicle → grenade launcher prohibited → switch back to AP pistol.

Then:

> Maintenance → weapon profile changes again.

That's terrible for the gameplay you're trying to create. fileciteturn52file1

I've removed that concept completely.

The fixed version does **not replace the selected weapon** when explosive mode is enabled.

Instead:

> Heavy Rifle stays Heavy Rifle.

> AP Pistol stays AP Pistol.

> SMG stays SMG.

> Carbine stays Carbine.

When that weapon actually fires, the script detects the weapon impact coordinate and creates a grenade-type explosion at the impact. ScriptHookVDotNet v3 exposes the relevant weapon/ped functionality, and `ExplosionType.Grenade` is part of the current enum set. ([github.com](https://github.com/scripthookvdotnet/scripthookvdotnet/blob/main/source/scripting_v2/GTA/Entities/Peds/Ped.cs))

So visually, your Genshin character can still be holding the **actual rifle you selected**, but the projectile impact becomes explosive.

That's much closer to what you were asking for:

> “Menyoo-style explosive ammo.”

Not:

> “Give my anime girl a freaking grenade launcher.” 💀

Fourth: I found a significant mismatch between your weapon XML and the C# loader.

Your uploaded `anyi.xml` is a **Menyoo 2.3.1 `<Loadout>` file** containing direct `<Weapon hash="0x...">` entries and weapon components. It does **not** use the custom structure:

```xml id="ci2dnt"
<Character>
    <Combat>
    <DriveBy>
```

Your actual uploaded file starts with:

```xml id="upvi7b"
<Loadout menyoo_ver="2.3.1">
```

and then directly contains weapon hashes. fileciteturn52file0

But the C# you gave me was expecting a character-based XML hierarchy.

That's why I don't want to pretend the old weapon loader was properly “based on `anyi.xml`.” It wasn't. It was loading a different generated `AnyiPartnerWeaponLoadouts.xml`.

And the log confirms this:

```text id="bpedgc"
Loaded automatic profiles: combat=7, driveBy=7, defaultCombat=3, defaultDriveBy=2
```

while your uploaded `anyi.xml` itself has no seven `<Character>` definitions at all. fileciteturn52file1turn52file0

So there was effectively a **weapon-library mismatch**.

I changed the source so it can recognize a direct Menyoo `<Loadout>` as well as the cleaner Anyi-specific format.

I also built a clean weapon XML from the actual hashes in your uploaded file.

**On foot → strong rifle as primary.**

**Passenger/drive-by → proper pistol/SMG.**

No grenade-launcher replacement.

Now about your **natural riding** preference. I changed this too.

Your latest script was actually using:

```csharp id="eeigir"
SET_PED_INTO_VEHICLE
```

for normal companion passenger entry. That's an instant seat warp. That is exactly what you said you didn't want anymore.

The fixed version uses the game's normal:

```csharp id="vgkpml"
TASK_ENTER_VEHICLE
```

for normal companion riding.

So the intended sequence is now:

> Anyi enters car → companion detects vehicle → finds free seat → walks/runs to vehicle → enters normally → becomes passenger.

Not:

> Anyi enters → POOF → anime girl teleports into seat. 😂

The code also has a small boarding-state cooldown so it doesn't repeatedly shout `TASK_ENTER_VEHICLE` at her every few frames. That's important because repeated vehicle-entry tasks can create exactly the slow/awkward boarding behavior you've experienced before. The current SHVDN task API supports vehicle-entry tasks and vehicle-follow tasks. ([wiki.rage.mp](https://wiki.rage.mp/wiki/Category%3AClientside_API?pageuntil=Players%3A%3AisTypingInTextChat))

And finally, I've added the **Convoy system** you were describing. 🚗🚗🚗

It's a new:

```text id="8x0gxq"
Anyi Convoy
```

menu with:

```text id="u5y52v"
Start Convoy — Cars
Start Convoy — Motorbikes
Stop Convoy
Recover Convoy
```

The important design is that it doesn't simply make the other partners run behind Anyi.

It searches for nearby suitable vehicles.

For Cars:

> companion gets a separate car.

For Motorbikes:

> companion gets a separate motorcycle.

Then the companion becomes the driver and uses GTA's vehicle-follow task to follow Anyi's vehicle instead of following Anyi on foot. `TASK_VEHICLE_FOLLOW` is specifically designed to make a vehicle follow another entity, with driving-style and speed parameters. ([wiki.rage.mp](https://wiki.rage.mp/wiki/Player%3A%3AtaskVehicleFollow))

And there's one really useful trick built into the convoy design:

If there are enough companions and the escort vehicle has a passenger seat, another companion can occupy that vehicle as a **passenger shooter**.

So with a situation like:

```text id="35va1t"
Anyi → Lead Car

Navia → Escort Car Driver
Clorinde → Escort Car Passenger / Shooter
```

you get a proper little convoy instead of three anime girls jogging behind your Lamborghini. 😭

The passenger can use the same drive-by combat system as the companions inside Anyi's own vehicle.

This also means the combat logic now recognizes convoy mode. Normally, a companion outside Anyi's vehicle is not allowed to participate in vehicle protection because we deliberately didn't want companions randomly running into tr

affic during normal driving.

Convoy mode explicitly overrides that restriction.

So:

> normal driving = only companions actually riding with Anyi participate in vehicle protection.

> convoy mode = separate escort vehicles are allowed to participate.

That's a much cleaner boundary.

One limitation I am intentionally keeping: a **single convoy driver cannot reliably both drive and perform a normal passenger drive-by at the same time**. The game's vehicle task system separates those responsibilities. That's why the convoy design tries to put a second partner into the passenger seat when the vehicle permits it. The current task API supports separate drive, drive-by, and vehicle-follow behaviors. ([wiki.rage.mp](https://wiki.rage.mp/wiki/Player%3A%3AtaskVehicleFollow))
